maintopic: FOURTH AND FINAL REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE
FOURTH AND FINAL REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE
speechtext:
I have the honour to present the fourth and final report of the special committee which was appointed to consider the procedure of this house. Copies of the report have been distributed to the members. There are quite a few points covered in the report, and if the house would prefer it I will try to explain it. The house might then be able to follow it more easily. The report is in three parts. The first part recommends permanent changes which should be made in the rules at this time. The second part recommends a change which should be tried on an experimental basis next year, and the third part sets out other matters which the committee has considered.
Part I recommends that the hours of sitting should be the same in future as they have
been during the latter part of this session with the exception that the dinner recess will be from six o'clock to eight o'clock p.m. There is also a provision that public and private bills will be dealt with on Tuesdays and Fridays from five to six o'clock in the afternoon instead of the former hour, which was from eight to nine o'clock on Tuesdays and Fridays. There is also a provision that on one of the days private bills will have priority, and on the other day public bills will have priority. With that report there is a recommendation that the necessary changes in the standing orders should be made immediately.
Part II recommends that the length of speeches should be 30 minutes instead of 40 minutes. However, I should point out that it does not recommend that the change should be made immediately in this rule, but recommends that it be tried out during the next session, or until otherwise ordered.
Part III sets forth other matters which the committee has considered but upon which a recommendation has not been made. The committee considered whether a debate should be allowed on money resolutions when the Speaker is in the chair, and also whether it is necessary for the minister in moving a money resolution to rise in his place and inform the house that the Governor General has been informed of and recommends the resolution to the consideration of the house. The committee considered, too, whether Mr. Speaker should leave the chair on Wednesday when there is a motion to go into supply or committee of ways and means. Hon. members will recall that at the present time, in order for the Speaker to leave the chair on Mondays, Tuesdays and Wednesdays to go into supply or ways and means, it is necessary to have a motion. The committee considered also the question as to whether estimates should be referred to a special committee or standing committees of this house. The general question of the structure of house committees was taken into consideration, as well as the question whether or not the rulings made by Mr. Speaker should be subject to appeal. Consideration was given as to whether those who are not limited to time in the length of their speeches should be limited as to time-
I shall read the last paragraph of the report:
Since your committee has thus far been unable to adopt the final report with respect to these proposals, and since other proposals may be forthcoming, your committee recommends that a similar committee be established as soon as possible after

House of Commons
the commencement of the next session to continue the consideration of changes that may be desirable to assure the more expeditious dispatch of public business.

maintopic: FOURTH AND FINAL REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE
speechtext:
The report is as follows:
The select committee appointed on October 9, 1951, to consider, with Mr. Speaker, the procedure of this house for the purpose of suggesting any changes that may be desirable to assure the more expeditious dispatch of public business, begs leave to present its fourth and final report.
Part I.
Your committee recommends that the standing orders of the House of Commons be amended as follows effective on and from the first day of the next session:
(a)	Standing order 2 is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"2. The house shall meet at 2.30 o'clock p.m. on each sitting day except Friday, when the house shall meet at 2 o'clock p.m. If there is not a quorum at the time of meeting, Mr. Speaker may take the chair and adjourn the house."
(b)	Standing order 6 is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"6. (1) At 6 o'clock p.m., except on Wednesday and Friday, Mr. Speaker shall leave the chair until 8 o'clock p.m.
(2)	At 6 o'clock p.m. on Wednesday, Mr. Speaker shall adjourn the house without question put, and the house will stand adjourned until Thursday.
(3)	At 6 o'clock p.m. on Friday, Mr. Speaker shall adjourn the house without question put, and the house will stand adjourned until Monday.
(c)	Standing order 7 is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"7. At 10 o'clock p.m. on Monday, Tuesday and Thursday (unless the closure rule is in operation) the proceedings under consideration will be interrupted, and Mr. Speaker shall adjourn the house without question put. Any proceeding not disposed of at the end of the sitting will stand over until the next sitting day when it will be taken up at the stage at which its progress was interrupted."
(d)	Standing order 15 is amended as follows:
"(i) In paragraph (3), the words '(From eight
to nine o'clock p.m.)' and the words 'Private and public bills, the former having precedence' under the heading 'Tuesday (Government Day)' are deleted and the following substituted therefor: "(From five to six o'clock p.m.) Public and private bills, the former having precedence."
"(ii) In paragraph (3), the words '(From eight to nine o'clock p.m.)' immediately before the words 'Private and public bills' under the heading 'Friday (Government Day)', are deleted and the following substituted therefor: '(From five to six o'clock p.m.)'.''

(iii) Paragraph (4) of standing order 15 is amended by deleting the words "9 o'clock" and substituting the words "6 o'clock."
Part H.
Your committee also recommends that, as an experiment for the next session, unless and until otherwise ordered, standing order 37 be considered as amended by the deletion of the words "forty minutes" as they appear therein and the substitution therefor of the words "thirty minutes," so that standing order 37 would for the duration of the next session have effect as if it were a sessional order reading as follows:
"37. No member, except the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition, or a minister moving a government order and the member speaking in reply immediately after such minister, or a member making a motion of "No Confidence" in the government and a minister replying thereto, shall speak for more than thirty minutes at a time in any debate."
Part HI.
Your committee has also given consideration to the following proposals suggested as possible means of expediting the dispatch of public business:
(1)	That when the order of the day is read for the house to go into committee of the whole on a resolution preceding a money bill, Mr. Speaker do leave the chair at once without question put.
(2)	That the practice of announcing in the house that His Excellency the Governor General recommends a money resolution to the consideration of the house be discontinued.
(3)	That whenever on Wednesdays government business has precedence, Mr. Speaker shall leave the chair without question put when the order is read for the house to resolve itself into committee of supply.
(4)	That the estimates be referred to a committee on estimates or to other standing or special committees of the house.
(5)	That the committee structure of the house be re-examined and reorganized.
(6)	That the rulings of Mr. Speaker be made conclusive and not subject to appeal.
(7)	That the speeches of those not now limited as to time in standing order 37 be limited as to time.
Since your committee has thus far been unable to adopt a final report with respect to these proposals, and since other proposals may be forthcoming, your committee recommends that a similar committee be established as soon as possible after the commencement of the next session to continue the consideration of changes that may be desirable to assure the more expeditious dispatch of public business.
Respectfully submitted,
W. Ross Macdonald,
Speaker of the House of Commons, Chairman.

maintopic: MOTION FOR REFERENCE OF REPORT TO COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE

speakeroldname: Hon. Alphonse Fournier (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: MOTION FOR REFERENCE OF REPORT TO COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
speechtext:
In all cases where substantial amendments to the standing orders of the house have been proposed in the report of a special committee appointed for that purpose, it has been the practice to consider the report in committee of the whole, and when the committee of the whole reports to concur in such report. In most cases when the report of the special committee was presented the motion to consider the report of the committee of the whole was moved without notice, either immediately or at some specified date. Concurrence in the report of the committee of the whole was moved immediately it was received, and in no case was any objection raised to this procedure.
At pages 702 and 703 of Beauchesne's third edition there will be found a Speaker's ruling dealing with a motion for concurrence in a supply resolution, which ruling is to the effect that it does not come within debatable motions under rule 17(a), now standing order No. 38. It is assumed that this would apply equally to motions for sending reports to committee of the whole. Now, the standing orders were amended in 1876, 1906, 1910, 1927 and 1940. What I have just said applies to those previous occasions. I know that I have to ask for unanimous consent of the house, but in moving this motion we have no intention of debating these changes in the standing orders this day. This procedure would just avoid the notice of motion. The tenor of my remarks today would, I believe, be sufficient notice that we intend to bring this matter forward as soon as the delays are over.
I move, therefore, seconded by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Harris):
That the house resolve itself into committee of the whole immediately to consider the report of the 94699-119
House of Commons
select committee appointed on October 9, 1951, for the purpose of suggesting any changes that may be desirable to assure the more expeditious dispatch of public business.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of ihe Opposition):
maintopic: MOTION FOR REFERENCE OF REPORT TO COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am as ready as anyone in this house to follow any course that is consistent with the proper dispatch of the business of this house and to expedite the proceedings. On the other hand, I do not intend to let the natural desire of every one of us, to have adequate time before Christmas day to make our own personal arrangements, to interfere in any way with what seems to be the best methods of dealing with business in this house. The suggestions that are before us on the one hand contemplate changes that have not been put in detail before the house in advance of this report, and it is not only the points that are raised but the points that are not raised that may be under consideration. For that reason, recognizing the fact it may well be that there would be some advantage in the members having an extended opportunity to consider this with others, I do not feel I could consent to this motion.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: FACILITIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Is he in a position to give a further report in connection with the availability of elevator space for wheat on the prairies? Is he able to say whether anything will be done by the wheat board to provide additional drying facilities for the damp wheat that is on the prairies? In particular, what is the situation now with regard to the allocation of cars in those areas that up to now have had a shortage?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: FACILITIES
speechtext:
The movement of grain,
particularly during the past thirty days, has been very favourable indeed. We have succeeded in getting the insurance period for shipping on the great lakes extended, and grain is still moving down the lakes at a time during which navigation is normally closed. This has improved space in the terminals at the lakehead. Stocks are down to about 32 million bushels at the moment, and grain is moving forward from the country in volume that is unusual for this time of the year, and will continue to do so for a period.
Some three weeks ago orders were put out that the railroads should concentrate on points where the congestion has been chronic for some time. That has been done, and I think there are very few points on the prairies that have not had a fair movement of grain. If there are such points at the moment they will receive immediate attention from the transport controller.
94699-119J
Inquiries of the Ministry
The problem of tough and damp grain is more serious this year even than last year. We were able to deal with the situation last year without any loss of grain through spoilage. This year the problem is much more difficult. It is being met in part by marketing tough grain as tough grain, which we have been able to do in a few countries, and we are concentrating on the drying of damp grain. It is impossible to bring in new drying equipment for terminal elevators which would be effective this year. We have looked into that, and by the time the driers are manufactured and installed the season will be over. So far as we can foresee I doubt whether there will be any addition to the drying capacity, but I can assure my hon. friend that the drying capacity is being used to the limit and will continue to be so used until the damp grain is disposed of.

The house resumed, from Wednesday, December 12, consideration in committee of Bill No. 17, to amend the Canadian Broadcasting Act, 1936-Mr. McCann-Mr. Dion in the chair.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE NUMBER OF GOVERNORS, PROVIDE PENSIONS AND FURTHER GRANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make some observations. First of all, let me say I support wholeheartedly the point of view expressed yesterday by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. Owing to the lateness of the session I shall not take the time to make any lengthy observations such as otherwise I would have made.
[Mr. 1

I must say, however, that my correspondence, and contacts I have with large numbers of people in my constituency, indicate a keen interest in this bill, and a general interest in the operations of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Correspondence I have received recently, as a result of study of the measure by the committee, shows that there is a general appreciation of the services rendered by the C.B.C., and the work it is trying to do. Therefore I am safe in saying that there is general support from people in all parts of my constituency, so far as the work of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is concerned.
In a constituency such as that of Kootenay West, there are many who to a great extent depend upon radio for their entertainment. They live in isolated mining communities and logging camps. Among their number are prospectors, trappers and the like. On more than one occasion I have visited trappers at elevations of 5,000 or 6,000 feet, living at perhaps a distance of twenty-five miles from a neighbour. They have told me how much they appreciate receiving the C.B.C. news and other features of the corporation, when they can tune it in.
Those people working in the hills, in the mines, on the traplines and as prospectors, as well as those in the lumber camps, are entitled to receive more consideration because of the work they are doing and also because of their isolation. They are performing an important service for the benefit of the country in isolated places.
I now take advantage of this opportunity to raise a question I have brought to the attention of the house on several earlier occasions, and that was brought to the attention of the committee which sat prior to the one the sittings of which have just concluded. I wish to say that the concern of many listeners in both Kootenay West and Kootenay East is that better facilities be provided so that they may hear C.B.C. programs at all times. I have received a number of letters recently about this matter which no doubt were stimulated by the investigation into this bill by the committee, and I have had the matter brought to my attention by a good number of organizations from time to time.
There are two local stations in the area. The station at Trail is an excellent community station and I understand last year it gave something in the neighbourhood of $20,000 worth of free time to the community it serves. There is another station at Nelson about which I used to receive many complaints. In fairness to that station I must say that it has improved its services. These two stations are low in power and, generally
Knowles.]

speaking, can only be depended upon to serve a limited area. A large number of the people in the northern sections of the Kootenays and in the isolated valleys are dependent to a great extent upon United States stations for their entertainment and news. This poor reception, most likely caused by the topography of the country, is particularly bad after nightfall. We are able to get some C.B.C. programs during the daytime from Trail, Kelowna, at times from Calgary and Vancouver, but after dark we are completely isolated from Canadian programs and must depend upon the United States stations.
As one who lives in the backwoods miles away from his neighbours I do not like to have to listen to the news according to Sperry's pancake flour, when other people are getting measured and objective news reports from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I think the manner in which news broadcasts are given by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is indicative of our national temperament and lack of hysteria in times of crisis. Repeatedly, people in my constituency as well as visitors have told me that they have been impressed by the objective reporting of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. As I say, many people have asked why something cannot be done to provide them with an opportunity of hearing our own Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
I am of the opinion that the general manager of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has some knowledge of my constituency, but officials in various departments have been inclined to look upon the Kootenays as being somewhat in the backwoods and possessing only a small population. Whatever their views may have been in the past, that situation has changed. The Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company are spending over $30 million on new developments. The mines in the area are spending another $10 million on new developments. Another $5 million is being spent on transportation and power facilities. Millions of dollars have been invested in saw mills and it is anticipated that an investment of over $70 million will be made within the next year or two in a pulp and paper industry.
All this means a great production of wealth and a large payment of taxes. According to Business Week, the Kootenays pay the largest amount of taxes per capita of any constituency with the exception of Westmount in Montreal. There will be an increased number of people working for the mines, the smelters, the lumbering industry and the future pulp and paper industry. I am making an appeal that something be done for the people of the southern interior of British
Canadian Broadcasting Act Columbia in order that they may be able to hear the programs of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
I am not a radio technician, in fact my mechanical ability is almost limited to oiling a wheel barrow, but people who know something about it tell me that we are not going to have satisfactory reception in the interior of British Columbia until a powerful station is located at Kamloops or at some other interior point. On occasion we can hear the Watrous, Saskatchewan station, which is a powerful station, and I am sure that it will require something of that nature to provide better service for the southern interior of British Columbia. I make this appeal to the minister and officials of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and urge they give consideration to this matter that has concerned so many people in Kootenay West and East for several years, and by so doing, recognize their needs and provide the proper service to that great and important part of this country.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE NUMBER OF GOVERNORS, PROVIDE PENSIONS AND FURTHER GRANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, notwithstanding the lateness of the session and the desire of many hon. members to bring it to a rapid conclusion in order to get home for Christmas I cannot resist the opportunity to say a few words on this important matter. It was my privilege to serve on the special committee on broadcasting, and as a new member who has been subjected to many experiences during the past few weeks, I must say that was the most stimulating and interesting experience of all. I have been interested in broadcasting, although perhaps not from the technical standpoint, for some time, and to come to grips with the concrete problems which face Canada in connection with this important matter was, as I say, a most stimulating experience.
I consider it most unfortunate that we should be pressed for time when we are considering this important subject. It seems to me that the whole field of broadcasting requires the maximum time for discussion so that we may clarify some of the confused thinking that obviously is present at the moment. As I took part in the discussions of the special committee I became increasingly aware of that confused thinking.
I consider this a most important topic because of the significance of radio broadcasting as a medium of communication in our complex civilization. Anything that plays a part in the communicating of ideas is significant. As has been the case with many other technological inventions and improvements, the attitude toward radio has been that it is a sort of panacea which will provide a
1866	HOUSE OF
Canadian Broadcasting Act universal solution for all our ills. The feeling seems to be that all you have to do in order to straighten out any problem is to organize broadcasting in the right style, put it on the proper basis and everything will be well.
It was so with newspapers when they first appeared on the scene. It was thought that with the advent of the modern press the problems of democracy would be solved because there would be provided an excellent medium through which public opinion could be moulded. Above all, in a democracy we must be aware of public opinion.
The first bright hopes have been dimmed as we witnessed the increasing power of the. yellow press in the hands of such journalists as William Randolph Hearst and Mr. McCormick of Chicago. This has tended to suggest that all is not sweetness and light so far as the use of this important medium is concerned.
I remember being involved in a debate as a young high school student on that old perennial subject of whether the pen is more powerful than the sword. I went around to all my fellow students and asked them if they read the editorial page, and did not get one affirmative response. That seemed to impress the judges because they awarded the verdict to our side. We were, incidentally, supporting "the sword".
Radio is somewhat different from the press. Radio deals with the spoken word, and the spoken word or oral tradition is more impressive in its effect than the written word. For example, the late President Roosevelt was able to exercise his tremendous influence on the people of the United States, notwithstanding the opposition of a good part of the press, because of his magnificent radio technique as demonstrated in the famous fireside chats. He could ooze through the ether right into the home. His ability in this regard was as significant as anything else in maintaining his influence in the United States.
We are well aware today, amidst the babel and confusion of voices, that the broadcasting medium is very important. I think perhaps here is where a good deal of the confusion arises in our thinking. There have been charges of blasphemous and indecent broadcasts and other kinds of nefarious activities over the C.B.C. during the present discussion. I think this partly arises from the fact that radio has come upon the scene very rapidly. Only yesterday the fiftieth anniversary of the first radio or wireless broadcast and reception was observed. I refer [Mr. Dinsdale.l

to the occasion when Marconi received the signal "S" across the north Atlantic. Radio has arrived on the scene very quickly and has developed rapidly as an accomplished technique just at a time of great social change and upheaval. Its significance in guiding and influencing human affairs of course has now become obvious. It was used with great effect under the nazi regime in Germany and the present communist regime in Russia. Therefore we who cherish freedom of speech and the other freedoms are very sensitive concerning the possibilities of the harmful influence of radio at the present time.
I have tried to be objective in this matter as I endeavoured to be objective in all the deliberations of the committee. I have looked through the scripts which were mentioned particularly and which were tabled for the members of the committee. I read carefully the speeches of Dr. Brock Chisholm, Mr. Bertrand Russell, Dr. Line, Dr. Hoyle, and so forth. This is not the first time I have encountered these gentlemen because they are standard fare on our university curricula. I recall making a feeble protest on the committee that one of the basic principles of academic freedom is that no restrictions be imposed with respect to the discussion of ideas. Perhaps I do not have to say this, but my own background so far as religion is concerned is of the fundamentalist variety. I deliberately projected myself into a study of the social sciences because I was somewhat alarmed from a layman's standpoint at a few of the ideas that were circulating. I wondered exactly what was involved in the new schools of thought that are growing up, particularly with reference to psychology, sociology, psychiatry and the social sciences generally.
As for Brock Chisholm, he is rather an extremist in the field, and I do not think he has been too influential since he became involved in the Santa Claus discussion some few years ago. Most hon. members will recall that he tried to criticize Father Christmas and stirred up a great tempest in a teapot as a result of carrying the Freudian idea somewhat too far. I was very interested in Bertrand Russell because back in the thirties he preached doctrines that were rather contrary to the best interests of the family, our basic unit of society. Bertrand Russell is a great mathematician and also somewhat of a philosopher. I think his line of thought has been practically discredited in the mind of anybody who has followed his ideas carefully because he is still a social evolutionist, and social evolution went down the drain

Canadian Broadcasting Act
with the advent of world war I, world-wide depression, world war II and the difficulties that have since arisen.
With respect to Dr. Line, I believe he is connected with the university of Toronto. I think I can highlight the approach that he takes by referring to a little incident that occurred to me personally. I met a student from the department of psychology of the university of Toronto who was a great zealot for the mental hygiene movement. The mental hygiene movement is doing a very effective job in solving one of our major social problems, the problem of increasing mental illness. But like all new things these men who come up with new ideas and new formulas go off the deep end and begin to feel that their particular idea is the supreme good for which man has been looking all through the long centuries of his upward quest. This student was most enthusiastic about the beneficial effects of the mental hygiene movement. He said: "If I could only go across the nation in a great crusade and tell everybody about mental hygiene I am sure that a good many of society's difficulties' would melt away". I said to him: "You sound almost like a religious fanatic in your enthusiasm for mental hygiene. You are attributing to the psychologist all the attributes of the Godhead, omniscience, omnipresence and so forth". He drew himself up very haughtily and said: "Are you not postulating God?" I think that is significant. I think it gets to the heart of the controversy in the struggle of ideas that is going on, the struggle of various ideologies for men's minds and souls during the disturbing times in which we are now living.
The farther I went in these respective fields of knowledge the more I realized their inadequacy and the more I realized that fundamental Christianity in the long run is big enough to smother and absorb any seeming inspiration or new viewpoint that might emerge out of these more scientific discussions. I do not think we need to be afraid of anything of that kind as long as we have a basic Christian philosophy, and as long as we endeavour to grasp the heights, depths and breadth of the wisdom that is involved in the Christian idea which underlies our western way of life.
If there is any danger at all from the threat of new ideologies I think it is because we have perhaps narrowed down our appreciation of Christianity to such an extent that it is not big enough to absorb the competition from these other ideas.
I would say something about the last script of Professor Hoyle's which was
definitely atheistic. I am in receipt of a communication from the Student Christian Movement which, while supporting the right of freedom of expression, makes this reservation:
We would, however, lay before you an additional request. It is true that while the broadcast in question did not deal in an explicit way with religion, some of them did proceed from assumptions that are antithetical to the religious and, more particularly, the Christian understanding of the universe and of human nature. While we would deplore any limiting of the freedom of expression of such points of view, we would, at the same time, request the C.B.C. to make provision for the presentation of the Christian position in broadcasts of as high a calibre as those being called in question.

speechtext: Was that not done with regard to Dr. Hoyle's broadcast?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE NUMBER OF GOVERNORS, PROVIDE PENSIONS AND FURTHER GRANTS
speechtext:
I think it was. I merely present that statement for the record. My viewpoint is very much the same as that presented in the communication from the Student Christian Movement. I feel that Dr. Hoyle's discussion was not relevant to the main theme that was established in these psychological broadcasts, and it is perhaps unfortunate that it was included in the series. However, I am not fearful for the ideological or spiritual well-being of Canadians so long as we can press home the basic facts of our own Christian viewpoint.
The difficulty is, of course, that we are all somewhat egocentric, and we look at the world from our own particular viewpoint. It reminds me of the elderly couple who were discussing the world as they saw it, and the gentleman said to his wife, "You know, sometimes I think that everybody in the world is a bit queer except you and me, and sometimes I think even you are a bit queer". I believe that is at the root of this problem of failing to appreciate the other viewpoint.
In our discussions in the special committee we were mainly guided by the report of the Massey commission. This commission has done a magnificent job for the advancement of arts and sciences in Canada. But sometimes I am persuaded to think the commission is a bit idealistic in its approach-and perhaps we need more idealism. It seems to support the notion that radio can be the panacea and solve all our difficulties if we only handle it correctly. I agree with the commission's criticism that the springs of culture are changing from the universities and the church and are now lodged in Hollywood and the radio and other mechanized means of communication. It is important that both of these sources of information, these sources of publication and communication, should cater to a higher level than that to which they have tended to cater when they are

Canadian Broadcasting Act
operating on a strictly commercialized basis. Hence the reason why I am basically in support of an institution such as the C.B.C.
But I do not think we are going to see any great upsurge in cultural interests as the result of that emphasis in radio broadcasting. It will be gradual, and I can agree with the Massey commission that we must move in that direction. I see no immediate possibility, however, of establishing a nation of highbrows, particularly in some of the outlying regions of this vast country of ours. I repeat that there is no technological solution, there is no technological panacea for the problems that are besetting our western way of life, both social and political. Today there is no simple, easy formula that will come to grips with all these difficulties.
We come now to the problem of broadcasting regulation which was a very controversial matter in the committee discussions. In order to present my viewpoint, I feel I shall have to refer briefly to the situation in the United States. I have pointed out that radio broadcasting there developed quickly and in a haphazard fashion. For example, I am told that from 1922 on, the popularity of radio spread like wildfire simultaneously in all countries. In the United States 90 per cent of the families in the northern states own one or more radios. Canada had over a million licensed sets in 1945, which was an increase of 450 per cent over 1934. Figures are similar for other countries.
There have been, perhaps, three distinct periods in the development of radio. As I say the development has been haphazard and without any direction, because it was an invention which appeared so suddenly. First of all, there was the novelty period from 1919 to 1922. Then it was regarded as a profit rainbow from 1922 to 1926, when the advantages of commercialization were seen. Then it had a period of adolescence from 1926 to 1936, when it came into competition with the newspaper advertising. Finally, it achieved success and became more or less established from 1936 onward. By then radio had stopped apologizing, and was a well-organized entity with a definite character. Radio advertising had gotten away from its earlier, primitive forms and had tended to become somewhat of an art, although we must confess there are still some of these primitive forms surviving, unfortunately. We have heard references to them during these discussions on broadcasting. No doubt a good deal of the experience of the United States in radio broadcasting has been that of perpetuating mediocrity. As we listen to the emotional contortions of the soap operas,
[Mr. Dinsdale.J
which is one of the frequent forms of program heard on the United States airwaves, some of us feel that radio broadcasting is far from being a mature medium.
It was the reaction to that sort of haphazard and uncontrolled development, when even too many channels were allotted to private broadcasting in the United States, that led to the B.B.C. complete state monopoly. Canada began to consider the problem back in 1929, and it was strongly influenced by both the United States experience and by the B.B.C. experience. During our discussions in the committee, I could not help but come to the conclusion that circumstances in broadcasting have changed rather remarkably since the Aird commission first made its report. At that time the conception was that broadcasting was a state monopoly, and there would be no private operators. Notwithstanding that fact, there are today 135 private radio operators in Canada. Admittedly they have all made a real contribution to radio broadcasting in this country. I have not stopped to examine why private broadcasting continued to survive, but no doubt it is due to the geographic nature of Canada. Notwithstanding the original intent of the Aird commission, we do have private broadcasting, and especially at the local community level it is doing a particularly fine job. It was obvious, as we listened to the private broadcasters' brief, that they are dissatisfied with the present arrangements for broadcasting in Canada.
It seems to me that the time has come when we might rethink and reformulate our attitude toward private broadcasting or toward broadcasting generally on the lines of some of the recommendations that have been made by the Canadian Association of Broadcasters. The press is taking up this theme. The Winnipeg Free Press has recently taken up the theme rather strenuously and is suggesting that some rethinking be done with regard to the basic philosophy towards broadcasting. I have here in my hand a clipping from the Winnipeg Free Press. Perhaps it would help if I were to put it on the record. It reads in part as follows:
For years the case for monopoly in broadcasting seemed overwhelming. So far as the layman was concerned it rested on technical arguments that a monopoly was inevitable, or if not inevitable, at least highly desirable. In Canada the threat ol Americanization through programs "piped in" tc Canada was also a very powerful factor.
It is, in fact, a very considerable tribute to the power of the idea of private enterprise in radio, diversification and independence, that in spite of the Aird commission proposal to close up or take over all private stations, and subsequent parliamentary studies strongly favouring the C.B.C., these private

stations have grown steadily in number and in revenue, which in turn reflects increased listening by the Canadian public.
The report goes on to indicate that as radio has grown up, as it has matured, as it has grown from a haphazard uncontrolled stage of development, we are beginning to alter our attitude towards radio broadcasting and are wondering whether under the present set-up we are not violating fundamental principles of freedom of expression.
This thought leads to the suggestion that has been put forward, not only during the present discussion but on former occasions, as to the desirability of an independent regulatory body or the other suggestion that has been put forward during these discussions, namely, that some sort of a joint planning committee might be arranged whereby there could be direct, constant, continuing liaison between the C.B.C. and the C.A.B. I am getting away from the terms of the present bill, but every time this subject is discussed and every time briefs are presented I think it is obvious that there is great agitation for development of this kind, and it would seem high time that some attention was given to these requests.
I was greatly impressed by one of the closing statements made by the chairman of the board of governors of the C.B.C., Mr. Dunton, when he said something to the effect that he hoped that parliament would define the radio broadcasting situation in Canada in sufficiently clear terms so that those engaged in the practical problems of broadcasting could get on with those practical problems, so that a state of relative stability would be established, making it unnecessary to be dealing constantly with those problems that have been emerging, particularly since 1936, the date I gave for the emergence of maturity in radio broadcasting.
I do not want to speak much longer, but I believe these are basic issues. The very fact that they are being discussed so frequently in the newspapers across the country and the very fact that they come up for discussion in the regular meetings of the committee on broadcasting indicate that they are real problems which must be faced constructively and directly in the near future.
I do not want to get launched into a general discussion of the problem of freedom of expression because that is a job for lawyers, and I will leave it to them. It is a topic however that should figure prominently in this debate.
In concluding, I might say just a word with regard to the licence fee. This matter was discussed in the committee and the impression
Canadian Broadcasting Act I received was that the problem of licensing radio receiving stations had become so difficult that it was hardly any longer a profitable venture. Recommendations were made by the C.A.B. and by some of the members that the licence fee might well be dispensed with. For example, we heard charges that the collection of the licence fee lent itself to techniques of racketeering, where unqualified licence sellers would approach unsuspecting householders and ask if they had bought their licences-of course, nobody ever knows whether or not he has a licence; I myself cannot remember. Because of the fear of being prosecuted, the householder would immediately buy a licence, whether he had one or not. That was one difficulty brought out. On the other hand it was pointed out that there are a large number of citizens who are never successfully apprehended and forced to pay their licence fee. I have here a quotation from the Globe and Mail of November 5, which outlines the situation in Toronto as follows:
It was announced recently that nearly 450 people were being prosecuted in the Toronto area alone, and that since last July, 1,800 delinquent owners who had failed to buy the 1951 licence had been found by house-to-house canvassing in this district by government inspectors.
If we got to the bottom of the problem, it might even be found that there would be in this chamber confessions similar to the one we heard recently with regard to smuggling, and that even some of the hon. members of this assembly are not in possession of their radio licences.
Most of the matters that I have discussed this morning are not up for review in the bill before us at the present time. But as one who had the privilege of serving on this committee, Mr. Chairman, I felt constrained to deal with them and to present, as briefly as possible, my own reaction to the situation.

We think that investigation ought to go forward until the subject has been exhausted; and the C.B.C. should be prepared to supply to the members of the House of Commons and to the committee on radio any and all information necessary to enable them to make up their minds about the matter. There are some features of the bill which we do not like, Mr. Chairman, but I am not going to discuss them now in detail. The discussion of them will be possible on the individual items. Before I sit down one thing I should like to say about the general policy or principle of the bill is this. I was sorry to note that no effort has yet been made to set up, for the purpose of regulating radio in Canada, an independent commission that is separate and distinct from the competing body, the C.B.C. We have been consistent in our belief that justice can never be done in this country to private radio and to the people generally until we have some regulating body that is separate and distinct from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, which is a competing institution in the field of radio. After all, we should remember that through the ages almost every advance-especially any advance in the fields of science-has been attacked as being against progress and contrary to religious beliefs. All sorts of accusations have been hurled at these advances. But in the end, in most cases the scientific principles have proven to be the truth. I think there is nothing we can lose if the truth is allowed to be expressed. If it is not the truth, it will not stand on its own feet but will fall by the wayside, provided that a free expression of opinion is allowed from all points of view.
We have advanced to a new high in civilization, or at least we imagine we have done so, by the formation of the United Nations since the last war. The United Nations has recently produced what is known as a universal declaration of human rights, and all member nations have subscribed to that declaration. Two of the articles which I will read would, I think, be a fair guide in governing us as to what is suitable and what is not suitable to be broadcast by our nationally-owned broadcasting system or by a privately-owned broadcasting system controlled by our government. Article 18 of the universal declaration of human rights reads as follows:
Everyone has the right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion; this right includes freedom to change his religion or belief, and freedom, either
Canadian Broadcasting Act alone or in community with others and in public or private, to manifest his religion or belief in teaching, worship and observance.
Article 19 reads:
Everyone has the right to freedom of opinion and expression; this right includes freedom to hold opinions without interference and to seek, receive and impart information and ideas through any media and regardless of frontiers.
If we govern ourselves by the principle that is expressed in these two articles, we will not be far astray as far as our public broadcasting is concerned. By saying that I do not for one moment mean that I would agree with all points of view expressed by anyone over the air; but if we confine ourselves only to the broadcast of opinions with which everyone agrees I am afraid these discussion programs would be pretty sterile affairs. Therefore I think a divergence of opinion is quite justified, provided that all points of view are expressed.
There is another point on which I wish to speak briefly, and then I shall conclude. I refer to the present set-up of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. As everyone knows, when the Canadian broadcasting system was brought into being in the 1930's the idea was that it should be set up as a state monopoly of broadcasting similar to the British Broadcasting Corporation, but in actual practice it was found not to be a practical thing, and as the Massey commission reports:
It soon appeared, however, that these pioneers in the field of radio broadcasting had made a place for themselves in their own communities and that they could perform important national services. It seemed therefore in the national interest that the C.B.C. should recommend the continuance of their licences and that they should be regarded as an integral part of the national system.
Therefore we have the situation where private broadcasters exist, and yet no provision had been made in the original legislation for their existence. We have the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in the position of being the parent of an unwanted child, if you wish. We have the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in the position where it realizes that private stations exist, but their existence was not planned in the first place. In actual fact a different set of circumstances exists now from those which were originally anticipated. Therefore I think we should not confuse ourselves by assuming that the private stations should be entirely controlled by the C.B.C. There has been a lot of confused thinking on this matter, and people have been led to believe that if a separate non-partisan body was set up to control broadcasting generally, to set down the regulations and to enforce

As a further admission that the existence of the private broadcasters is justified the Massey report goes on to say:
In this broad country we still have inadequate radio coverage; without the supplementary outlets of the private stations many more areas would be deprived of the national programs of the C.B.C., and could be reached only at great additional public expenditure. As I said, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is in the position of being the parent of an unplanned and unwanted child, and finds itself in the position of being torn between mother love on the one hand and embarrassment for the very existence of the private stations on the other. As far as the laying down of regulations and their enforcement are concerned, I would suggest that the control should be in the hands of a separate and non-partisan body, as are the railways. Because this report not only recommends the continuation of the control, subject to the right of appeal, but it seems to feel it desirable that the control should be exercised more authoritatively than in the past.
I read from page 284 of the report where it says:
In 1936, the C.B.C. was constituted-
There it is, you see; the birthday is 1936. Evidently the earlier date was a kind of illegitimate birth, which has been forgotten.
l'n 1036, the C.B.C. was constituted to "carry on a national broadcasting service within the Dominion of Canada" . . . the only status of private broadcasters is as part of the national broadcasting system.
It is important to remember that phrase, because we come to that line of reasoning again and again. Then, referring to private broadcasters, the report continues:
They have no civil right to broadcast or any property rights in broadcasting. They have been granted in the national interest a privilege over their fellow-citizens, and they now base their claim for equality with their "business rivals" on the abundant material rewards which they have been able to reap from this privilege. The statement that the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is at once their judge and their business rival implies a view of the national system which has no foundation in law, and which has never been accepted by parliamentary committees or by the general public . . .

Canadian Broadcasting Act
We. are resolutely opposed to any compromise of the principle on which the system rests and should rest.
I am not going to enter into any argument with the Massey commission on points of law. All I wish to do is to introduce the much humbler ground of common sense.
At page 283 the report lays down the following principle-and here you have the same continuation, the same kind of argument which flows all the way through this report:
The principal grievance of the private broadcasters is based, it seems to us, on a false assumption that broadcasting in Canada is an industry. Broadcasting in Canada, in our view, is a public service directed and controlled in the public interest by a body responsible to parliament.
Let us examine this bold and categorical statement which the Massey commission makes. Can the Massey report, by an ex cathedra statement of this kind, alter existing facts? Surely the truth is that radio broadcasting is, in one of its aspects at any rate,
. an industry. It is one of the most important industries, the dissemination of news which is becoming, we are assured, increasingly more important. When they speak about there being no property rights, it has been well pointed out by those who have examined the situation closely that at the time of the invention of printing there was no property right in it, either. In some countries it was converted into a state monopoly, or it was placed under the church and subjected to licensing. It was only gradiually, particularly in the democracies, that property rights in printing and publishing were recognized!, and made free from licensing and censorship.
Surely it is correct to say that radio is a most potent industry, when it is an agency for the dissemination of news. Then, if the C.B.C. is to continue to control the news, are we not practically turning the clock back and returning to the situation of hundreds of years ago, by putting the dissemination of news under licensing and censorship?
It is not necessary to say, what I believe to be the fact, that up to the present time the corporation has exercised this right with restraint and, I think, with a sense of co-operation. I am assured by fair-minded private broadcasters that that is so. But my first comment is that if the power is a bad power, liable to abuse in the hands of men who are not moderate, then it is folly in the highest degree to continue it merely because at the moment it may be exercised with restraint and control. That is not all. I am not suggesting today that, merely because I am assured it is exercised in the main with restraint and consideration, there is not


a great deal of evil connected with it even now. Let me read again from the Massey report, page 27, as follows:
The board of governors retains its control over air channels and programs. This it does in two ways: first, through its power to recommend to the Minister of Transport the grant, renewal or cancellation of licences, and second, through its power to regulate the nature and amount of advertising, political broadcasts, and in general, the character of all programs broadcast in Canada by any station.
I believe that power is having a considerable restraining effect even at the moment. The power outlined there is not a wishy-washy power; it is a power of life and death. It would be entirely unrealistic to suppose that the people in any private station faced with this power would feel that they were not in any way affected. I am informed by well-informed people that it is a mere statement of fact to say that every broadcast over a private station is more or less conditioned by the fear of offending the government. The C.B.C. has the power of life and death over every broadcasting station. As I said, if people have the power of life and death it does not matter much whether they exercise it in a nice or a nasty way. I remember reading an essay somewhere on murder, I think it was by De Quimcey. The author said that he "once knew a bulldog who had murdered a brother bulldog with pleasing circumstances of good taste". I suggest that it is not going to be at all helpful to the private broadcasters if this power of life and death is used even in the most pleasant of fashions. The fact that you give a cigarette to a man who is going to hang makes no difference, because he is hung all the same.

I should like to ask the committee to examine for a moment or two the nature of this new agency for the dissemination of information. As the London Economist points out, it is the greatest invention since the invention of printing. The Massey report, on page 23, indicates that Dr. James Thompson, for a short time acting general manager of the C.B.C., referred to radio as being a new device of singular potency for entertainment, information and public persuasion. Does not that phrase "public persuasion" raise inescapable questions as to whether this device of singular potency for entertainment, information and public persuasion should be in the hands of a corporation which to all intents and purposes, so far as control is concerned, is a monopoly?
Does anyone believe that however much it is desired to create an independent corporation, however genuine the officials are in their desire to be absolutely independent, they are not absolutely independent, that the corporation is still, when all is said and done, a creature of the state? Yet the Massey commission, far from deprecating this control, recommends that it should be more vigorously exercised and in that way gives it a kind of additional respectability, I suppose.
Let us look at this for just a moment from the point of view of freedom of the press. Someone has pointed out that anyone who can hire a printing press and buy sufficient newsprint can publish, a newspaper, that he does not have to ask the government's permission. But anyone cannot operate a radio station. For one thing we are told that the frequencies are limited and have to be rationed. An informant tells me that that reason is rapidly disappearing as science is overcoming the shortage and we are going to have an abundance of frequencies, if we have not already.
Even if the reason advanced of the necessity for allocation is a valid one, it does not follow that the C.B.C. needs to be invested with power over what the private stations shall broadcast. The situation in the terms of the dissemination of news has been well pointed out by a man, I think he is a newspaper man, who said that it is as if newsprint were so

If anything like that were done of course it would at once arouse vehement protests, and yet I suggest- I do not think it can be contradicted-that something like that is implied in the power of the C.B.C.
I am utterly unable to understand why the C.B.C. should desire to continue with this power and why the government should be so anxious to have them continue. I would have thought that they could do what, it seems to me, is their real job much better if they did not have this other job to do. It seems to me that that is not their real job and it is one which they should not have at all. I think they would be extremely well advised to divest themselves of this, and I believe it would add to their public support.
It is interesting to note that when radio first came into existence it was placed under the Department of Marine and Fisheries. Apparently no one was very interested in the child and perhaps there was a spare office in that department. That was the way it went. For some years it sort of bounced about and then it was recognized for the great and overwhelmingly important thing that it was but it was some time before it was realized that an invention comparable to printing had been discovered.
I think it would be the height of folly if, because we are ready to praise, as I am, the C.B.C. for the work which they have done and for their enlightened attitude on aesthetic and intellectual development, we were to overlook the fact that here we have a tremendous potential danger to the freedom about which we talk so much. It does not need much stretching of the imagination on the part of anyone to see someone at the head of the C.B.C. who would regard it as childish folly not to use the C.B.C. in times of a general election. I have said already that I believe that those at the head of it are doing their utmost to avoid that. I repeat what I said a moment ago, that we would be foolish to deny the possibility that we might have a very different kind of people and a very different kind of time. Of course everyone knows that radio has been the greatest weapon that dictators have had. I remind you again of Dr. Thompson's words, that it has "singular potency for public persuasion".

One writer pertinently asks whether a public corporation is ever completely protected against political considerations. I should like to refer ' to a statement of Sir Frederick Ogilvie. I do not know anything about him except that he was the second director general of the
B.	B.C. For all I know he may be the world's greatest reactionary, but it does not worry me in the least. I want to quote a statement he made in February 1946, and members can make up their minds whether or not his words are correct. He had this to say:
Monopoly of broadcasting-*
I will come back to that point. I realize that technically we have not a monopoly, but I am suggesting that broadly speaking we have something equivalent to a monopoly. Sir Frederick said:
Monopoly of broadcasting is inevitably a negation of freedom, no matter how efficiently it is run. or how wise and kindly the board or committees in charge of it . . . The B.B.C. itself, good as it is, would gain vastly by the abolition of monopoly . . . The only possible losers would be the various governments of the day-Labour, Tory, coalition or whatnot. Governments are thoroughly suited by the charter as it stands. What better could any government wish for than to have at the end of the street a powerful efficient instrument which has all the appearance of independence but which by the existing provisions of the charter and licence it can control at will.
As I said a moment ago, technically that is .not our situation. We have private stations but they are under control of the
C.	B.C. I have tried to indicate what I think that means.
There was one thing which bothered the Massey commission and that was facsimile. They seemed to feel that in the case of facsimile there was some danger. It did not fit in with their picture of complete independence. They realized that freedom of the press was involved and their suggestion was that state regulation should be confined to technical matters. On page 292 of the Massey report they ask this question:
How can full liberty be assured to this new form of newspaper production without doing violence to the national broadcasting system?
Further on they say:
. . . we can see many grave objections to imposing upon it the limitations necessary for radio broadcasting but inapplicable to the press. It would seem to us both desirable and practicable to ensure that the potential development of facsimile take

place in an orderly manner and at the same time the traditional freedom of the press be left unimpaired.
What I utterly fail to understand is why the Massey commission, saw the danger there and seemed to think it was confined to facsimile. I think one can only say that they had developed a superstitious kind of worship of the phrase "national broadcasting system", that they seemed to think it had been constructed in heaven and that no one here should lay impious hands on it.
My suggestion is that the argument which led them to stop, look and listen in the matter of facsimile and to try, though perhaps not very effectively, to suggest a way out of that difficulty, should have led them to raise the same question and be troubled by the same doubts with respect to the much broader situation. For that reason I think they were wholly wrong in recommending that these powers be left to the C.B.C. I can only hope that these considerations, which I believe are serious, will not be brushed lightly aside. I should like to say a few words, Mr. Chairman, which, if they do not have much to do with radio or the C.B.C., may have some relevancy to this discussion. With all due respect to the C.B.C. and radio, I think perhaps my subject is even more important. I should like to say a word or two on the question of freedom, and its application to the pursuit of truth. No doubt we are all united in that we do want to pursue the truth. The trouble is, of course, to find out what is truth. It is an age old question. The nearest I can ever get to it here, I think, is by an application of my intellect to my environment, my environment including as it does creeds, ideologies and opinions of all kinds. Then having examined those I must make my choice.
I am not here condemning any particular programs, nor am I advocating any particular programs, but I do assert, and assert vehemently, that speech must be free. By the same token listening must be free. In short, the intellect must be free to make the choice which I have indicated. If we restrict the freedom to listen, then we are indulging in the very same type of authoritarianism which we deplore in certain other countries. We who hold the majority opinion cannot deny the right to the minority to express theirs. There has been mention here of the influence of what has been termed by one hon. member as "bad programs" upon young people. I have had some experience with young people, both my own children and other people's. I should like to state my own position in that regard. These people have upon them the influence-I am now speaking of my own children-of the home. They know the religious opinions of that home, they know our political opinions, and I hope they will be able to form their own opinions about those things. We hope, of course, that they will be guided by our example. Let me make it clear that it is only a hope, and not an insistence. The only pressure which has ever been exerted upon them so far as I am concerned, or ever will be exerted upon them, is the pressure of what I hope is a good example.	.
Sir, the child is a new individual. I do not believe the mere fact that he is my child gives me ultimately the right to warp or twist him. He is a new individual and, may I say, a new soul. He must make his own choice. I would encourage him to look; I

Canadian Broadcasting Act would have him listen to everything. I would have him see everything and examine everything, and then bring to bear his intelligence so that he may make his own choice. My responsibility in the matter is to guide him along what I believe is the proper road, and to provide him with a good example. My responsibility is to see that he is equipped with the ability which he requires to make his choices. I have tried to be open-minded. I do not attend only the political meetings sponsored by my own party. I' go to Conservative meetings, to Liberal meetings and to Social Credit meetings when the opportunity is offered. Let me say that I have learned something from them, and that is why I go. I want to see if there is something I can learn. I do not go there with my eyes and ears closed and with my mind made up.
Let us come to radio, which I might mention incidentally. If there is any control over it, it must be control by a public body which in itself is controlled by this parliament, because parliament represents all the people of Canada. If that applies to radio, it applies with more force to television whose potentialities for good or evil, for vulgarity or decency, are even greater than those offered by radio. In passing, I might say I am well pleased with the C.B.C. on those points, particularly when one considers the difficulties with which that organization has been faced, and which it has done its best to meet. I believe that people at the head of that organization feel their responsibility in regard to the quality of the programs. I believe that when the C.B.C. is not so dependent as it is now upon commercial revenue, it should be able to raise the standard of the average program put out by the corporation.
Now, as to political programs, religious programs or other programs of a controversial nature, I believe they should be in the hands of a body which is prepared to allow all sides of the problem to be aired. This opportunity must be granted, or otherwise this vaunted freedom of speech will be limited by the amount that one is able to spend upon it. In such an event the scales would be heavily weighted in favour of those organizations or individuals who have great funds to spend upon the propagation of their own ideas. These people should have no more privileges on the air than those of less financial means.
I, sir, am not greatly impressed by a doctrine whose holders are not prepared to submit it to argument and public scrutiny. If it is a good argument, a good cause or a good belief, religious or political, it will stand upon its own feet. On the other hand, if those

Christianity have been drawn into thL debate. I do not like to make a parade ot these things, but in so far as I am a Christian -and I hope I am a Christian-then I am a Christian not through coercion and not through fear. I am a Christian by my own choice.
Personally I do not think that the doctrine as espoused by the Sermon on the Mount has anything to fear from its detractors over the air or anywhere else. There was no freedom of speech accorded to the early Christians who founded the Christian faith. It is my contention that although they were a minority group, they were entitled to such freedom. Yet in my hon. friend's view they were a minority group. They were a group of revolutionists, as a matter of fact, who were rejected by the majority, despised by orthodoxy, and persecuted by the money changers; and their leader indeed was crucified. But nevertheless they went on to change the face of the world. That last expression makes me think of John Buchan who, as all hon. members will recall, was for a time Governor General of Canada. He said:
The spark, once transmitted, may smoulder for generations under ashes, but the appointed time will come, and it will flare up to warm the world.
May I say that such spark should not be extinguished, for where there is no spark there can never be a flame.
Finally, let me draw one thing to the attention of some of my hon. friends who think that any opinions with which they do not agree should not be put over the air at public expense. Let me remind them of what Voltaire, with whom I violently disagree on many things, once said in a famous letter: "I disapprove of what you say", said he, "but I will defend to the death your right to say it". That sums up very succinctly and concisely my own opinion with regard to the demand for freedom in its relation to the search for truth.

My hon. friend the
minister has over and over again stated that the national system is not in competition with the private stations. If it is not in competition with the private stations there is no reason why the private stations, being commercial stations, should not use the type of programs and the type of advertising that they choose without at the same time influencing the national body or the national institution. The very interruption that my hon. friend makes indicates that there is a competition for business as between the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the private stations, and rather intensifies the demand that hon. members have made over the years; and certainly it underlines the need that where there is competition there should be an independent body to determine the respective rights and authorities of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the private stations with whom they are in competition. I think the minister, by that very interruption, has given one of the best

Canadian Broadcasting Act arguments why we should have an independent body, designed to assure and preserve that degree of competition as between the national body and the private stations which today is denied when the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is in the position of being competitor, lawmaker, judge and jury in regard to all matters in controversy as between the national body and the private station.
Indeed, I was most impressed by the opinion given in the minority report of Mr. Arthur Surveyer, which is to be found in the report of the Massey commission. In his report he asked for the setting up of a regulating body to determine in a semi-judicial manner the controversies as between the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the private stations. I am not going into detail at the moment, but I suggest that the amendments proposed in the bill before the committee are merely makeshift. While they appear to set up a semi-judicial or judicial right of review, that is restricted entirely to the rights of the private stations, when a question of law is at stake, to appeal to the exchequer court when a licence of the private station has been suspended or abrogated. The amendment does not cover the field referred to by Mr. Surveyer in his minority report. All it does is to permit the right of appeal on a question of law, not fact, where a private station has had its licence suspended or abrogated.
I cannot understand the attitude of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in being so opposed to an independent body being set up. The Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways are in competition for freight and passenger business. By his interruption a moment ago the minister indicated that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the private stations are^ in competition over advertising. That being so, where there is a class of interests such as that, surely however well intentioned the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation may be, human nature being what it is, it cannot determine rights as between itself and those with whom it is in competition.
I know this argument will not be accepted, because the stand of the minister and those who preceded him in that position during the last ten or twelve years has been one of very strong opposition to such a body being set up. Nonetheless, as a result of the weight of public opinion, the government has seen fit at least to assure the private stations the right of appeal when deprived of their licences either temporarily or permanently, but that in turn is restricted only to a question of law. What does that mean?

How many appeals will ever be made under that section? If the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation cancels the licence of a private station on -the ground that it has failed to live up to a regulation passed by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, that is a regulation as interpreted by the lawmaker, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, there will be no right of appeal. This right of appeal on a question of law is so restricted as to be almost a nullity before it is actually passed by parliament. I am going to suggest to the minister that the right of appeal should be widened to cover not only the questions of law but also questions of fact, so that justice may be assured when and if a private licence is suspended or abrogated either permanently or temporarily.
I now come to one further matter, namely the question of television. Those of us who live in other parts of Canada than Quebec and Ontario have a justifiable complaint that we are to be denied even the prospect of the likelihood of a hope of having television within the next ten years. Montreal and Toronto are to have television stations, but Winnipeg and Vancouver are given a rather nebulous promise that sometime in the dim future stations will be established there. Is television to be held back in this country because of the fact that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation does not desire, for reasons which it knows, or by reason, of difficulties over which it has no immediate control, to give it to us? Are we t-o be denied television when there are available private companies, and I believe private Canadian companies, willing and able to provide television in different parts of our country? Somebody has asked: Are we to allow United States companies to come into Canada and establish television? I only hope the same desire to maintain the development of our country had been characteristic of governments in the past. Our country is being developed; these great oil fields in western Canada are being opened up and are available to Canadians who have initiative to go ahead, yet they were allowed to remain dormant until financial interests in the United States came into our country. I would like to see Canadian companies given an opportunity to establish television in this country; for surely we are not to be held back for years just because the national policy at the moment denies to private companies the opportunity to expand and develop an industry that is rapidly becoming one of the great industries across the line.
How long have we to wait? Well, there is an article in today's Globe and Mail regarding

the television station that is being built in Toronto. It says:
Canadian television programs which, a year ago, were set to begin this fall will not go on the air before June at the earliest, a C.B.C. official said yesterday.
He gave the reason as lack of steel priority and the like. Then he announced this:
A Canadian television network is far in the future.
The article goes on:
It was indicated that licences for private TV stations will not be granted until C.B.C. has a national service.
Now we know, if that C.B.C. official who spoke yesterday in Toronto represented the policy of the C.B.C., that as far as western Canada is concerned, until a national system has been established-and at the rate the C.B.C. is going that is a long, long while in the future-no consideration will be given to the granting of licences to private companies. This is a retrograde step. It is a denial of the type of expansion we need in this country. If private industry is prepared to develop and expand this very necessary mode of communication in these modern days, then surely if the C.B.C. is not in a position to go ahead those of us in other parts of Canada should not have to wait until such time as a national system is set up before consideration is given to the applications of private companies.
Those are one or two considerations which had not been discussed at length, and which I thought should be placed before the committee. I believe the C.B.C. is doing an outstanding job; but that does not mean there is no room for improvement. That does not mean the C.B.C., in its policy on television, should be permitted to stagnate development in this country that would take place if at least the applications for licences by private companies were considered.
Furthermore this policy of stagnation in television is driving Canadians in cities along the border to the United States to secure the kind of programs Canadians have the right to expect in their own country. That would be bearable, were the policy of the C.B.C. such that, while granting priority to the C.B.C., it would not deny to private companies and to the people as a whole the right to the kind of service people across the line receive from private enterprise.
