Mr. Chairman, as a member of the committee on the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation I believe I should make my position clear, especially after the speech of the hon. member for Saskatoon. I thought some of his remarks were intended for me, or for others among my friends who have been advocating that this or that script should not be broadcast over the C.B.C.
I must say that the officials of the broadcasting corporation have demonstrated a full comprehension of our attitude as expressed

Canadian Broadcasting Act in committee. We dealt specially with the scripts of Dr. Chisholm, Dr. Ewen Cameron, Dr. Anna Freud and Dr. Carl Binger, as well as with those of Dr. Bertrand Russell. I shall not discuss all these this afternoon, because I do not wish to delay the discussion.
Let me say, however, that it is not because we do not believe in freedom of speech that we asked the C.B.C. officials not to permit the reading of those scripts on the air. It is because we thought they were wrong. And we thought they were wrong because they advocated policies, for example, such as that of birth control. We ask those who, in the name of freedom of speech, are ready to permit the spreading of those ideas on the air whether, if such a policy were accepted and put into force by the governments of the world, we would be a free people.
It is all right to speak about freedom; but it is easy to be enslaved by having too much freedom, especially when the ideas expressed are wrong. The hon. member for Saskatoon said he did not want to twist or force his children into believing this or that. Well, I do not attempt to give him a lesson in bringing up his children. Such a thing would be far from my mind. But for myself, if I am to be charitable toward my children I believe I have to keep away from them everything that could harm them physically, intellectually, spiritually or morally.
I use the word "morally" with a purpose, because I believe when we permit the expression of the theory of Freud by this or that speaker over the air, then they are expressing an immoral idea. And if immorality is not wrong, then I must ask myself-as all hon. members will-what is wrong? It is immoral to advocate that our children should have no control placed over their sexual appetites. Those ideas have been expressed by some speakers who advocate the Freud philosophy. That is the stand we took in the committee; and we think we were not wrong in asking that normal, sensible ideas be expressed over the C.B.C. and the privately owned stations.
When we ask that the C.B.C. be more careful in the choice of its commentators or moralists, I do not think we are wrong. When we ask that truth be given priority on the air, I do not think we are wrong. I do not think it has been expressed before that truth is relative. Truth is one and indivisible. You cannot have two truths. It is impossible. We do not like to have these principles advocated.
It is all right to say that our children should be free to listen to anything on the radio and form their own opinions. We may think we are right in saying that, but we are wrong because our children have not been
[Mr. Gauthier (Portneuf) .1
prepared to assimilate, to digest and to separate a dish of good food from a dish of poison. They cannot differentiate because they have not been prepared. That is why we ask that a proper selection be made of the scripts used by the C.B.C. I do not think we are wrong or too dogmatic in expressing our views in that regard. It is all right to say that one who expresses a good idea should not be afraid that it will come to naught. Communists were a minority but we allowed them to express their ideas everywhere and distribute their literature. Their philosophy was immoral, but it spread just the same. I am not at all afraid that the principles of the faith in which I believe will be endangered by communist principles, but I say it is not right for a public man to try to do away with the possibility of harm being done to the wax-like intellects of our children. We should not let them listen to everything and try to digest it themselves, especially when they are not prepared. It is our duty, it is the duty of the professors in our colleges and universities, to prepare them.
We should not permit ideas like those advocated by Freud to be spread among our younger population with the possibility of our young people becoming sex maniacs, That is why I got up in the committee the other day to ask that this kind of Script should not be used by the C.B.C. I am a supporter of the C.B.C., as I think they are doing a good job. But I think they have also been a little careless. Canadian Broadcasting Act between freedom of the air and freedom of speech on the one hand and a licence to abuse and insult on the other hand. There is quite a difference. I think the teachings of Brock Chisholm, Bertrand Russell and the rest of them belong in the universities. When a young man or young woman matriculates and enters university I think their minds are mature enough to differentiate between the teaching they got from their fathers and mothers and whatever religious body they may have belonged to and the teachings of the people to whom I have referred. I think they are able to sift the good from the bad in what Brock Chisholm, Bertrand Russell and others are teaching. I do not think it belongs on the air.

I should like to remind hon. members of an item that appeared in the press a few days ago. It said that 50 per cent of the freshmen class at McGill university were so immature that they did not know who the Prime Minister of Canada was. They thought the Secretary of State for External Affairs was the leader of the opposition. That is not my statement; it is a press statement. It would not be a bad idea if the C.B.C. were to institute a series of lectures to build up the institution of parliament in the minds of the Canadian people. Parliament is taking a pretty bad beating in the press, over the air and in many other ways. Boys and girls who were smart enough to go through high school and enter university apparently do not know very much about the institution of parliament and democracy as we understand it. I think the C.B.C. should put on a program series to try to build up parliament in the minds of the Canadian people, particularly the young people entering our universities because they are the ones who will be the leaders of tomorrow. If they come out of university with minds filled with the teachings of Anna Freud- and Brock Chisholm, the future of Canada is going to be a rather doubtful proposition.
All through the discussion of programs so far as television and radio are concerned I have heard it said that we have to build up the culture of the country. That is a matter of definition. When I listen to Brock Chisholm, Anna Freud and these others, and the debate in the house today, and see the beating the institution of parliament is taking and the ridicule to which members are subjected, I am reminded of the propaganda disseminated in Europe in the twenties and thirties which led to the rise of Hitler. Hon. members will recall that the Hitlers, the Goerings, the

Canadian Broadcasting Act Schachts and the rest of them were going to develop a new culture in Europe. They were going to develop a super race. Their philosophy was based on the teachings of Nietzsche They were going to make Hitler God. All the mythology of the past in the form of religion was to be stamped out. The totalitarian mind is very impatient when it comes to bodies such as the House of Commons, which move slowly. They want the right to move fast and to say they are going to do this and that. This insidious process came into being in Europe, and we should be careful when it comes to determining the cultural requirements of everybody in the country to see that we are not just absorbing a whole lot of the philosophy that has been disseminated throughout the world over the last twenty years in an effort to break down democracy and displace the institution of parliament.
I have sat and listened to all the debate and, mind you, I am just one of the proletariat. I do not consider myself to be very cultured. I think the dictionary definition of culture is that it is a matter of manners, intellect and taste. I know many well-mannered people who are very intelligent but when it comes to a choice between listening to a C.B.C. radio play on the death of Socrates or Amos and Andy, they will pick Amos and Andy. If we believe in freedom then we should have freedom of choice. We should not have something jammed down our throats from coast to coast on a Sunday evening, when people have time to sit down and listen, for which we do not care very much. Having in mind the definition of culture and the classics of the past, it took us a couple of hundred years to get around to saying, "Where are you going?", rather than "Whither goest thou?"
If you try to impose all the limitations and cumbersome methods of doing things in the past on a modern fast-moving world it is not going to work. I should like to know, for example, how many people would listen to a Shakespeare play, or look at it on television, while the Grey Cup final was being broadcast. There would not be very many. When we instituted our radio system I never thought it would be a straight educational and cultural organization moulded to conform to the ideas of any one individual or half a dozen people. The universities and schools are there for that purpose, and people can make their choice of what they want to study.
So far as I am concerned, I visualize radio and television largely as mediums of entertainment. I think that is the purpose for which the average person buys a radio set
[Mr. Gillis.l

and for which he will buy a television set. The great majority of our people left school when they were in very low grades. They are not going to sit in their homes and have heavy Shakespearean plays and that kind of thing thrust at them which most of them do not understand, and no matter how often you keep shoving it at them they will not understand any more about it. They believe and I believe that radio and television should be largely designed to provide entertainment. I know there is a place for education. I enjoy the forum broadcasts very much. In my opinion they are a valuable asset. I listen to them whenever they are on the air. I do not care what the subject is. If two or three people on such a broadcast are discussing a question, then that is educational. You have got three sides of the question in most cases, or two sides with a chairman in the middle keeping the thing in balance. There is a lot of value in such broadcasts. People can understand that kind of thing, but when you take a man like Brock Chisholm and put him on the air with his theories on psychiatry you are only getting one side of the question. There is no debate and no discussion.
In my opinion it is largely wasted, because I do not think the average person in this country is interested in that subject. The great majority of them do not understand what he is talking about. All the evidence I have had as to the value of it has been against it. I have had letters protesting that kind of thing, but I have never had anyone write to me and say we should continue it. I do not believe we should remove it from the air, but I suggest to the C.B.C. that any time Bertrand Russell or Brock Chisholm is to go on the air the program should be like a forum so there could be a discussion of both sides of the subject. I believe the C.B.C. is wrong in putting it on in the manner they have been following.
There are medical doctors in this house, and they know that psychiatry is going directly into that field. The psychiatrist has about as much respect for the medical profession as he has for religion. They believe it is a case of mind over matter. I had one experience with psychiatrists, and if the theories they expressed on these broadcasts were no better than the experience I had with one of them in the veterans affairs department, then I do not think very much of them. When the last war was over the government relegated most of the boys who came out of the service with nervous breakdowns-psychopaths or whatever you want to call them-to the regular insane asylums.

This was done on the advice of the psychiatric department. This department said you could not be good to these fellows because they would never get better. On the advice of this psychiatric division these fellows were put away. Their wives and families were outside without any allowance, and these men were to be cured by leaving them in the institution. Their wives and children were left outside to starve to death.
We had the head of the psychiatric division before the veterans affairs committee at that time. I do not want to be disparaging, but I questioned him for a long time and I never saw a person more in need of a psychiatrist than he was. He stood there and tore a pocket handkerchief into about a thousand pieces while he was talking to us. I do not suppose he even knew he was doing it. I was not impressed with his theories. The government eventually took care of the matter and realized that the wife and children had to eat, regardless of whether or not the man was going to get better. I am not impressed by these theories. I have been the sort of fellow who knew he had to learn a lot, so I have read a lot of that material. It has not changed my opinion about anything. I agree with the hon. member for Macleod that the best teachers for the children of this country are the fathers and mothers in the homes. If the basis of a strong character cannot be made there, then neither Freud nor Brock Chisholm is going to do very much afterward.
I was brought up in a church. I have gone through life, and it has been a rather rough life, but I have never seen anything that changed any of the basic beliefs I learned there. In all the ups and downs of life those basic principles I learned when I was taught my catechism in my church have held constant and still hold good. Any time I hear a person talking about having a Christian philosophy, and at the same time belittling any religious body, I do not believe him. I think everyone who is a Christian finds his beliefs in the same basis. In my opinion all the Christian churches go together; you cannot separate them. I am not in a position to give advice to the hon. members of this house, but I have lived for fifty-five years and I have seen a lot of this world, and I suggest that anyone who has watched events for the last twenty years will realize that we want to be a little careful about our desire to expand freedom of that kind to make sure we are not giving licences to a lot of people.
Let us stop for a moment to think about the trade union movement in this country
94R99-121
Canadian Broadcasting Act and in the United States. No organization in North America has greater respect for freedom than the trade union movement. What do you find the heads of the three congresses doing within the last couple of years? They realized the danger of subversive activities, and they had to use some discipline. They had to get a measuring stick to determine where freedom ended and where licence, abuse and vilification started. These congresses threw out some large bodies of unionists as a disciplinary measure to impress some small groups at the top who persisted in using their positions for the purpose of undermining everything for which the movement stood. I am suggesting to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation that they have a great responsibility to the future of this country, as have the newspapers. When they are thinking and talking about this business of freedom, democracy, preserving peace and all the things which we are building an army to defend, our language should be as moderate as we can *possibly make it. This institution of parliament should not be held up to ridicule as it has been on a good many occasions in the last couple of years.
When controversial subjects are being dealt with, such as the one about which we are talking-and it is controversial because it hits at the very roots of society-rather than having one man on the air for half an hour the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, recognizing that it is controversial, should have someone else there to take the other side of the argument. The program should be a forum. I do not believe in stopping anyone from expressing his opinion, but I feel that with subjects such as this which are highly controversial care should be taken that they are presented in such a way that the people listening have an opportunity of balancing one statement against the other.

speechtext:
I have greatly enjoyed the contributions of the various members in respect of this whole matter, Mr. Chairman. At the beginning of the discussion my remarks were rather inclined to be nonconstructive, but I should like to say something of a constructive nature now.
As other hon. members have so well said, I believe that all the points of view on all subjects, religious, political or other kinds, ought to be given an opportunity of being heard. I believe in freedom of speech to the fullest degree. Our position is that no particular philosophy or interest originating propaganda should be given free play to establish its particular notions consistently and consecutively without adequate reply.

Canadian Broadcasting Act
If we might refer to our friend Brock Chisholm again for a moment or two, I would say that apparently we are discussing his particular freedom to use the air. I wonder why Brock Chisholm should have any more freedom to use the air than any of the other several million mature men in Canada.
I do not think he has established any right above the rights of other people to have his opinions freely expressed. Then is Brock Chisholm speaking for someone else? Is there some interest behind Brock Chisholm which is seeking for freedom of expression? I am afraid that is the case, although I hope it is not.
I said this morning some fairly strong things, and I meant them; and I will say them again any time they need to be said. But I should like to put on what I said this qualification, which I thought unnecessary at the time but which I certainly had in mind. I do not mind having Brock Chisholm come into my home and express his views freely if I can be in my home and have just as much time as he has to put forward the other side. Let us take, for example, the evolutionary theory. I should be quite happy to have him discuss before my family-and they are the most precious possessions I have in life-the evolutionary theory if I can be there to say: "Now, look here, friend, have you read Sir Ambrose Fleming's "Origin of Mankind"? Are you aware that this book completely subverts your evolutionary theory? Have you read "The Bible is True" by Charles Marston, published in 1934? Do you realize that that destroys completely the grounds for your attitude of higher criticism toward the bible, as does also "The Bible comes Alive" published in 1937 by the same man? Do you realize that Sir Ambrose Fleming is backed up by Lecomte du Nouy in his "Human Destiny" and by Sir James Jeans, one of the very best scientists in the world?"
If I can have the time to put those things before my family in his presence, or before anybody else's family, I have no anxiety because Brock Chisholm and all the men believing as he does can be utterly torn to shreds by men who are as well informed as they are on the other side of the subject they are discussing. But to put him up there with a free hand for fifteen, twenty, thirty or forty minutes, with no chance in the world for anyone to answer him, is something that I say is almost necessarily the abnegation of true freedom of speech.
I rather incline to the ideas expressed by two or three hon. members whose names I have forgotten for the moment; the hon. member for Cape Breton South was the last one. If we are to discuss for instance the
matter of what to do about the rapidly increasing birth rate in certain parts of the world, let us plan a town meeting of the air. Let us have three or four men who are qualified to talk about the matter. Let us meet and prepare thoroughly, as I know men do when they are going to have a town meeting of the air, and let us have somebody there who can present the alternative to the reckless idea Brock Chisholm is endeavouring to establish in the minds of the people. Then I would have no anxiety at all.
I would rather like to hear Brock Chisholm on the air if you could put alongside of him a man who knew how to deal with him; and there are plenty of those. I would not hesitate to stand before him at any town meeting of the air or on any platform; and there are plenty of people who could do the job just as well as I could.
Mr. Chairman, I thought it was probably well to say what I have said, in a manner, closing off what I said a little while ago. I still agree with exactly what I said, but I would put this little modifying speech alongside the former one, as giving the C.B.C. something constructive to work on rather than only what would be destructive.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I merely want to make one or two remarks on this subject. I think the debate has been extremely interesting. It shows one thing, namely the danger of a central government organization in radio, and the extreme danger lest we in this chamber set ourselves up as censoring what the Canadian people shall listen to. That is a dangerous trend. I do not think it is part of the job of a parliament to state what shall and what shall not be listened to. I merely mention that point because of the same dangerous trend which I see in these discussions.
The mass media of the radio and the moving pictures are failing to interest people, in my opinion, largely because of what I shall call infantilism. They are playing down to the most juvenile type of intellect you can imagine. As a matter of fact, somebody said to me the other day that the moving pictures have now been developed for the average teen-ager of seventeen or eighteen. I fear that radio has ceased to be the force it once was. I note this trend in the major urban centres. It is ceasing to be the force it once was because it is constantly appealing to a lower and lower intellectual level. That may be a good thing or it may be a bad thing; I do not know. But I know that the interest in radio has definitely slackened-that is, shall we say, in the more or less intellectual side of radio-in the major cities or urban centres.

I now want to make an observation with regard to the report of the Massey commission. on this subject. The commission regarded with approbation an association known as the Canadian writers' committee. I was interested in this matter because I used to know some of the people who belonged to Canadian authors' guild. I tried to find out who this Canadian writers' committee was. All I could learn about them was that they were an ad hoc organization brought together apparently for the purpose of making this submission. As far as I could find out it consisted of Dr. Frank Scott, a man called Len Peterson and somebody called! Bissell working at the university of Toronto. Dr. Frank Scott is well known for his socialist views for which I respect him but with which I disagree. Len Peterson is a commentator on the C.B.C., and is employed more or less full time by that organization as a free-lance writer. I could not find anything about the third member of this so-called writers' committee.
It seems that the difficulty in accepting views advanced on this subject-and of course it would be the difficulty of any royal commission-is that they have not been able to get the opinion of the ordinary man in the street with regard to the whole question of radio. Perforce they have to accept, and do accept, the opinions of those who I suggest in this case are prejudiced witnesses, who have every right to their submission and every right to their prejudices, as each one of us has; but I disagree that they represent either Canadian writers or the Canadian reading public. These facts should be brought out. The problem is of very great importance.
The rural parts of Canada are very much more dependent upon and more interested in radio than are the urban parts. I think that would be borne out by any survey of the listening habits of the Canadian people. We have to be most careful in bringing down opinions on this extremely controversial subject. For example, I heard that when the federation of agriculture brief was given it had not been submitted to the general meeting; and as a matter of fact a man called Howard Prentice was refused the opportunity of being heard by the federation and by the committee because he disagreed with that brief. Therefore I suggest that when we are considering this whole matter of radio the report we have in front of us, while it is sincere, is nevertheless apt to be based on the opinions of prejudiced witnesses. Therefore it must be considered in that light.
I am not going into the question of private radio stations, because that has been dealt with very adequately by others. I do wish 94699-1211
Canadian Broadcasting Act to emphasize that unless the intellectual standard of radio is kept up, some fear that it will go the same way the moving pictures were going until they began to take hold of themselves, by basing its appeal on the adolescent mind and the undeveloped mentality. That is the greatest danger we face today in radio programs in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this discussion on second reading of Bill No. 17 has assumed a rather broader latitude than I had expected, although I have no criticism to offer of that in particular. It was thought that by referring this whole matter of radio broadcasting to a special committee perhaps time would be saved and there would be more complete examination of all matters having to do with radio.
The committee did have the advantage of information given to it by the officers of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and of representations made by outside interests and by those who were interested in radio privately. Although it is not my intention to speak at length on the whole question of radio, because that has been dealt with pretty much in the abstract here yesterday and today, the submissions 1 made upon the resolution preceding the bill and upon second reading of the bill put forth as clearly as I could, and perhaps in as much detail as might be expected, the position of the government and of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, so it is not my intention to go into more detail and to make any kind of a lengthy speech.
At this time I do want to congratulate the committee on radio broadcasting on the excellent work they have done, and to thank them for their deliberations. It afforded an opportunity, as I said before, of getting in detail both the criticism and the suggestions of those who were interested in radio. During the years in which I have taken an interest in this particular subject I do not know that we have had a better committee than the one which examined into that subject this year. I am like the hon. member for Brandon who spoke today, who said that he found the work very interesting and very stimulating. That was exactly my reaction to it years ago on the first radio committee that I attended. I think that has been the reaction of some of those hon. members of the house who have sat on this and similar committees having to do with radio broadcasting. Therefore at this time I want to take the opportunity-and it may be the only opportunity I shall have-to say thanks to the members of the committee, and to commend them for the excellent work they have done.

Canadian Broadcasting Act
Among the things the radio committee did, which I think was of great advantage, was to visit Montreal and see our Radio Canada building. That was well worth-while. I think it was an eye-opener to the members of the committee to see the physical side of what goes into both television and sound broadcasting. It surely must have given them some tangible demonstration of what the costs are in radio, because, as was pointed out here yesterday, when you see a mobile unit for television with four cameras that cost in the neighbourhood of $100,000 you can well imagine what all the equipment costs. On the floor on which the mobile unit was located there was a million dollars worth of television equipment which was ordered by this country a year ago last May from the Marconi people in England. I was in their factory and saw some of it in the process of manufacture. When one sees a building of that type with its splendid studios, its great control board, the equipment and machines for making recordings, as well as all the other equipment, and couples with that the highly-paid officials, he can readily understand why the cost of radio, both sound radio and television, is as high as it is.
On December 4 the radio committee made its second report, at which time it reported Bill No. 17 to the house. The committee considered the bill carefully, and it has been reported to the house with only one slight amendment. The final report of the committee is expected shortly, and I am sure it will give expression to what have been the results of the deliberations of the committee, and will set out its recommendations.
The suggested changes in the act, with which we are now dealing, are those based upon the Massey report. Let me say at once that in my judgment whether we agree with it or not the Massey report is one of the finest, probably the finest report we have ever had. I say that because the commission went into great detail, took great pains to cover the whole country and to invite people to make submissions; and it did all these things to a much greater extent than any other commission we have ever had in this country dealing with radio.
Having set up the commission, and as a result of the representations made to it, the government is guided by those recommendations which go to form the report itself. I was surprised to hear the hon. member for Greenwood deal almost entirely with the Massey report. Evidently he is not very favourable to it. I hope there has been no rift between him and his friends. Perhaps he was only laying the basis for some friendly


family arguments over the Christmas season. He referred to this being the fifteenth anniversary of radio, and dates it back to 1936, when the Canadian Broadcasting Act was put into effect. He said it was a matter of regret that a former prime minister of this country and his government, who were in power from 1930 to 1935-and he was referring to Right Hon. R. B. Bennett-were not given credit for having implemented the report of the Aird commission. Well, about the only people I have heard casting any discredit upon that right hon. gentleman have been members of his own party. The reason they find themselves in the position they are in today is that they repudiated the political philosophy of that right hon. gentleman and his government, when they held office between 1930 and 1935. The hon. member would like to get away from that and start out on an entirely new basis.
The section in the Massey report dealing with television states:
In radio broadcasting Canada experimented with a purely commercial system before changing to a national system.
Right Hon. R. B. Bennett changed that system on the basis of the Aird report, which was made at that time. I suggest to the committee that no sensible leader of the government, no matter what party he might be leading, would have followed a different course. It was clearly indicated that that was the course in the best interests of the people of Canada, and that was the course the people would endorse and would follow: a policy of national ownership and a nationally operated radio system. So I say the difficulties are principally based on the fact that his own party at this time is not following what was laid down by Mr, Bennett at that time.
The growth of radio in Canada has not yet achieved all for which we might hope in a national system. I quote again from section 80 in the Massey commission's report, where they say:
It is still young. It has had to struggle against poverty, inexperience, and the physical obstacles of this difficult country, But, as we have suggested in part I and have stated here in language as clear and unambiguous as we can command, we are convinced that the existing Canadian system of broadcasting has served the country well in the past and offers the greatest hope of national unity and enlightenment in the future. We urge that the national broadcasting system be given the power and resources sufficient for its great national responsibilities.
Could there be any stronger recommendation than that? It is a recommendation, not made without deliberation, not made in haste,

but made by the top men of this country, investigating it after years of deliberation and study.
There have been a number of criticisms by several hon. members which perhaps were just and legitimate, but which I believe can be answered shortly. I think it was the hon. member for Eglinton who, referring to the Canadian association of broadcasters and the recommendation that we should have a regulatory body, was critical of our present system. I would point out to him that the evidence before the committee shows that the Canadian association of broadcasters has shifted its ground very much within the last few years. What they want now is a regulatory body only with reference to the technical aspects of radio, and that to come from the Department of Transport. I suggest there is nothing to gain if they are going to attempt to wreck the set-up in the Department of Transport, just as throughout the years they have attempted to break down the system we have had under the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
The hon. member was critical, too, of our television policy. This afternoon he referred to the fact that applications for television licences had been made back as early as 1945.

speechtext: They might have been before that, so far as I know.

speechtext:
Well, some bright individual may have had an idea twenty years ago, or perhaps ten years ago, that a franchise would have some monetary value for him, and that television would come into being in this country; and for that reason might have put in an application. But, to go back even as far as 1945, I suggest such a person would not have had the slightest idea at that time what it would cost to set up television.
We have been criticized for being dilatory or slow in enunciating a policy and putting it into effect. I suggest that the action of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the government in that regard has saved the people of this country millions of dollars. In 1945 or 1946 one could easily have formulated a policy and attempted to implement it, and the result would have been that what was purchased at that time would have been obsolete by this date. Three years ago I accompanied the governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to New York where we studied the matter of television. We were shown by National Broadcasting, Columbia and private interests what they had done. They told us that they had spent $50 million up to that date and that most of it had been
Canadian Broadcasting Act spent to no avail. We have profited by the progress which has been made in television.
As far as issuing of licences for television goes, I have been told in private conversation that not one single person or group of persons is prepared immediately to spend money to go into the development of a private television unit. It would cost at least $500,000 for a set-up, and any group would have to be prepared to spend probably another $500,000 before they would reach the operating stage. A further cause for delaying the progress we would like to have made has been the shortage of materials for transmitters, steel for towers and the other things that go into the building of a television station. All these are in short supply, and we are in no better position than private persons or enterprises in making application to the steel controller. We do not get any preference in that regard.
I should like to say a word with reference to the much discussed matter of controversial broadcasting. I am going to put on; record what I thought was a very good article which appeared in Saturday Night of December 15. The C.B.C., the Prime Minister and myself and I presume many members of parliament and of the government have received all kinds of correspondence with reference to the controversial broadcasts. A great many people objected to them, while many more commended the freedom of speech that had been allowed by the C.B.C. One is put in the position of deciding whether he should recommend closer censorship, or whether the freedom which has been exercised for years should be allowed to continue. This article reads:
This journal shares very fully the view, which is now being expressed by a good many organizations of national or provincial scope, that there should not be any further restrictions imposed by statute on the character of the material which may be sent out over the air on Canadian wavelengths, beyond those which have been in force ever since the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation was set up to regulate radio in Canada. These restrictions leave to the C.B.C. a very large freedom as to what it will broadcast and what it will not broadcast, and on the whole that freedom has been exercised for some fifteen years with great judgment and direction.
I think that is most significant. The article then goes on to discuss in some detail the broadcast given by Hoyle, the astrophysicist, and it has some criticism to offer with respect to that. It then continues:
But we do not for a moment suggest that the fact of our differing with the C.B.C. in this instance is a reason for fettering the C.B.C. for all time with a statutory prohibition against certain proscribed ideas, or still worse, against certain proscribed broadcasters.
We believe that there is a difference between radio and other forms of communication, and that the proposition that any and every idea has a

Canadian Broadcasting Act right to communication on the radio in the same way as it has a right to communication in print or in an assembly, provided only that it is not indecent, seditious, libelous or calculated to promote disorder, is untenable.
I agree with that. It goes on:
But we believe that parliament would be most unwise to attempt itself to distinguish between those ideas which may be broadcast and those which may not, and still more unwise to hand over a general power to do so to a board of censors whose chief concern would inevitably be to allow nothing on the air which could possibly be the object of any protest.
I believe that in connection with these controversial broadcasts there should be an opportunity for reply. I would think also that the broadcasters or commentators ought to have sufficiently good judgment to say nothing that would be either insulting or offensive to the Christian religious beliefs and sensibilities prevalent in this country. I think censorship to that extent might very well be employed. It is not very often that we have criticism of that type in connection with the C.B.C. I am bound to admit that in this particular instance probably something got over the air which it would have been better for the great majority of our people not to have been permitted.
This morning the hon. member for Kootenay West referred to the needs of the southern interior of British Columbia. I feel quite sure we can assure him that when this bill goes through and our financial position is better than it has been for a number of years it will be the policy of the C.B.C. to greatly expand its facilities and that part of British Columbia will be looked after. I do not know that there is anything to be gained by taking up further time that might well be given to a consideration of the details of the bill.

It will be recalled by the committee that a grant of $1,500,000 was made to the C.B.C. last spring so that if this section is adopted it will provide the C.B.C., along with the grant made last spring, with an annual grant
iMr. McCann.]

of $6,250,000 over a period of five years. This provision happens to tally with the recommendation of the Massey commission, to be found on page 293 of the report. They indicate that the corporation will annually require, in order to carry out its program of expansion and for other purposes, the sum of $14,200,000 in all. The C.B.C. has stated that in order to maintain services even at their present level it requires about $3 million a year in addition to its current income of approximately $7,500,000. If all the local and less desirable national commercial programs are dropped, the corporation will require an additional $1,500,000-some $14,200,000 in all.

I do not think it is germane to my purpose. I referred to the fact that the section did happen to tally with the report. I am not interested in the balance of the section for the present purpose.
The income of the corporation during the past fiscal year was $8,301,000. The addition of $6,250,000 to that sum would give the corporation something close to $15 million of revenue in the present fiscal year. The commission did contemplate that the corporation would submit to some reduction of its commercial revehues as a result of the elimination of some of the commercial broadcasts.
The income for the fiscal year ended March 31,	1951, was drawn from three
sources. The first was licence fees, and I will give only round figures. The amount was $5,572,000. Then there was commercial broadcasting, $2,463,000; and miscellaneous, $266,000, or a total of $8,301,000. I am going to digress for a moment to draw attention to one feature of that statement of revenues. In his remarks a few moments ago the minister apparently sought to create the impression that Mr. Bennett, in fathering the Canadian Broadcasting Commission out of which the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation later grew, was committing himself and his party for all time to a nationally owned, nationally operated, national monopoly in radio broadcasting.
I do not think that is a fair interpretation at all of the views of Mr. Bennett. It is one thing to create a national system. It is quite another thing to say that there shall be on the one hand either no other type of broadcasting carried on in Canada or on the other hand that if broadcasting is permitted under other auspices, namely private auspices, the national system shall have the power of regulation, what together with the licensing powers amounts in fact to the power of life

and death over these other outlets for broadcasting. But let me point out this further fact that the Aird commission and the whole scheme of the Canadian Broadcasting Commission as conceived by Mr. Bennett rested upon the assumption that the commission would not go into the field of commercial broadcasting, that their programs would be free of commercial features, and that the commission would be dependent upon public moneys or licence fees for its income. With the approval of this government, however, there has been a steady departure from that basic principle of the original scheme of national broadcasting in Canada, and it is to little purpose indeed for the minister to picture the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation today as being the fulfilment of the dreams of Mr. Bennett on the one hand, and then shut his eyes to the fact that the financing of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation-yes, and in many respects the type of program it is giving-has departed very materially from the original conception of the Canadian Broadcasting Commission and national broadcasting in Canada.
I wish to offer some comments on the matter of the income of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.	It will have been
noticed that the C.B.C. at the present time is drawing approximately $21 million per annum from commercial broadcasting. The report of the Massey commission, which obviously commends itself to the government, recommends that the corporation should eliminate much of the revenue it is deriving at the present time from commercial broadcasting.
I should like to refer to page 291 of the report where the majority make this recommendation:
That the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation refuse all commercial programs not acceptable in content and that they consider the possibility of eliminating some of the less desirable commercial programs now carried, and of replacing them by programs more appropriate to Canadian listeners.
The recommendation in the minority report of Dr. Arthur Surveyer at page 399 should commend itself to the house. He says:
There is no doubt that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should be granted whatever amounts are needed to maintain an adequate service both in broadcasting and telecasting for the purpose of fulfilling the aims of the Canadian Broadcasting Act. Although the expenditures of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation appear reasonable when compared with those of the British Broadcasting Corporation, the commission does not know whether or not the operations of the corporation are efficient, nor if substantial savings could not be realized by entrusting the production of commercial programs to private producers.
That leads me to say that, far from there being no competition between the national system on the one hand and the private
Canadian Broadcasting Act stations on the other, there is very keen competition. You have very keen competition to the extent to which the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation permits competition on the part of those private stations which are its competitors. Competition for commercial revenues is direct and keen. Private stations have complained to the parliamentary committee that while they ask nothing of the Canadian taxpayer and must finance their operations entirely from their commercial revenues, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, on the other hand, while receiving the entire licence fee on receiving sets, nevertheless at the same time competes with them for revenue in this field of commercial broadcasting.
It should be clearly understood that if this substantial grant is to be made to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation it should be upon the condition attached to its recommendation by the Massey commission. That recommendation was that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should be prepared to forgo a good deal of its present commercial broadcasting. It will be the right of the people of Canada if this grant is made to expect better programs on the C.B.C. and to expect fewer and less objectionable commercial features. I think that is the wish of the officials of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I wish to say that in fairness to them, but it seems to me it must be clearly understood that if this house is going to vote this large additional income to the C.B.C. it must attach that condition. I point out to you, sir, that such a condition does not appear in this legislation. There is no suggestion in the bill as it appears before the house that a condition of the kind recommended by the Massey commission is attached to this grant of additional income.
I come to another of the principal sources of revenue to the corporation today, licence fees, which last year yielded an income of $5,572,000. This income was obtained from the $2.50 licence fee on 2,212,000-odd receiving stations in Canada. I say "receiving stations" because one should not regard a receiving station and a receiving set as synonymous. A person may have more than one receiving set at a receiving station without requiring more than one licence. I point out to you, sir, that if this section passes we are not only committing parliament to a principle but to a very definite figure by way of parliamentary grant. That carries with it implications which I consider are of very great importance. I suggest that now that parliament is committing itself to this principle the time has come for the elimination of that nuisance tax, the licence fee on receiving stations.
1898	HOUSE OF
Canadian Broadcasting Act I point out certain factors in relation to this $2.50 fee, some of which were the subject of evidence before the parliamentary committee. In the first place, whatever may have been the situation when that $2.50 licence fee was first imposed, I think it is a very different situation today. The fact of the matter is that today the benefits that are derived as a result of the operations of the C.B.C. bear no relationship to the fee. Everyone with a receiving set must pay that fee whether or not he listens to the programs of the C.B.C. The fee does not bear any relation to service.
In the second place the amount has no relationship to fact. It does not cover the cost of operation of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
In the third place, and I wish to develop this point, the collections of this fee have been very troublesome. I do not believe one member in this house will have the temerity to say that collection is complete.
The Massey commission in its majority report had this to say at page 294:
The Department of Transport considers that the present method of collection is reasonably effective and thorough. However, if the figures of the dominion bureau of statistics are to be accepted, Canada's three and a half million private receiving sets which should be licensed ought to yield over eight and a half millions a year in licence fees instead of something over five million.
As was mentioned in the committee with regard to these licence fees, the fee is levied in terms of receiving stations and not simply in terms of receiving sets. There is a lot more in this discrepancy on which the Massey commission has placed its finger, however, than can be explained away simply by referring to the people who own more than one receiving set. I d'o not think the contention put forward by the officials of the Department of Transport charged with responsibility for the collection of this fee is very convincing when they say that collection is satisfactory. As I said a moment ago,
I do not believe there is a member in this house who will have the temerity to say there has been universal or 100 per cent collection of this particular nuisance tax.
How many people who ought to be paying this tax are not paying it? No one in this country can answer that question. Even amongst those from whom collection is being obtained great difficulty is being experienced. The principal official of the Department of Transport for this particular subject is Mr. Browne, controller of communications. In his testimony to the committee on December 6, he said there are 120,000 to 150,000 people in this country who never pay their licence fees until late in the year. If you refer to a table he filed with that committee you will 

find that there is a great deal of tardiness on the part of many of the people who do pay. For instance, last year in the months of April and May 47-2 per cent of those who eventually paid remitted their licence fees, yet the fee is payable on April 1. The percentages for the remaining months are as follows: June, 21-5 per cent; July, 8-6 per cent; August, 7-4 per cent; September 4-4 per cent; October, 4-1 per cent; November, 2-4 per cent; December, 1-5 per cent; January, 1-4 per cent; February, 0-7 per cent; March, 0-8 per	cent.	That is not	the kind	ofrecord that suggests	that this is	the sort	of
fee that is either collected easily or paid readily by those upon whom it is imposed.
I say to you, sir, that this is an extremely costly fee to collect. What would we in this house say if the Minister of National Revfenue came to us and	said	it cost him	over 12 percent to collect	the income tax,	or over	12
per cent to collect the excise tax? We would throw up our hands in horror at the very idea, and say there was something fundamentally wrong if it was costing that much to collect these taxes, and that we ought to re-examine the whole situation. The fact of the matter is that for years it has cost over 12 per cent on an average to collect this tax, and last year it cost 12-2 per cent of every cent that was collected. If that cost had been charged directly to the proceeds of the tax you would have realized a net of 87-8 per cent. I say this is a shockingly high cost of collection, and the house ought to face up to that fact.
This year parliament has appropriated over $700,000 just to provide for the collection of these fees from which a revenue of something like $5,600,000 is expected. Parliament is throwing a lot of good money away, in my submission, in seeking to collect a tax that is unpopular and that is extremely difficult to collect. As you know, some time ago it became necessary to send people out, supervisors and others, from door to door canvassing for licence fees. These people were paid on a commission basis. In the committee a member asked Mr. Browne why one should introduce the principle of commission into the collection, of taxes or fees imposed by parliament, a principle that would take us back to the abuses of the Roman empire. The answer was that when the department paid these people a salary they did not go out into the sparsely settled areas, but confined themselves to the built-up areas where it was comfortable to go about. I believe that is another factor which calls upon parliament to examine whether this nuisance tax ought to be continued any longer.

I think it would be interesting to the house to know that last year the government depended upon 346 house-to-house canvassers for 38-3 per cent of all that was collected on account of this nuisance tax.
The next factor in this connection which I should like to mention is the matter of prosecutions. This $2.50 licence fee is imposed by regulation pursuant to power given to the government under section 4 of the Radio Act. Many hon. members in this house, Mr. Chairman, may have forgotten that the further provision in section 4 of the Radio Act provides for the imposition of a fine of up to $50 or three months' imprisonment for any person failing to pay this fee. Just weigh that against the amount of the fee that is sought to be collected, and the difficulty in collecting it. The fact is, as has already been mentioned in this debate, that many people quite innocently do not know whether or not they have paid their fee. It is not something that comes to their mind like income tax returns. Many innocent people could easily overlook the payment of this licence fee. Yet any person who is in that position, however innocent he may be, is subject to a fine of $50 or three months' imprisonment.
Last year there were 13,830 prosecutions, and the result worked out in average figures in this way: The average fine was $3 and the average costs imposed $3, a total of $6.
The procedure in connection with prosecutions is very clumsy. A prosecution cannot be started locally without reference to Ottawa. At Ottawa a particular bureau in the Department of Transport sifts through these recommendations, with all the consequent delays. In the face of this situation, sir-an unpopular tax; a nuisance tax; a tax that is hard to collect; a tax that is not universally enforced and cannot be, I submit; a tax that has clumsy provisions attached to its enforcement -what did the Massey commission say? The Massey commission, made some comments on this subject and they criticized in the language I have used the present collection of tax. While the Massey commission did not come up with the kind of recommendation I think they should have brought in for the abolition of this tax in favour of the parliamentary grant, they nevertheless criticized in. the words I have used the present degree of enforcement.
In the light of the criticism contained in the majority report of the Massey commission I think it would interest many hon. members to know exactly what the Department of Transport now proposes. In the first place, sir, it proposes-as we were told by Mr. Browne in the committee on December 6-that there
Canadian Broadcasting Act should be an amendment of the Radio Act to provide for a minimum fine of say $10 for anyone found operating a private receiving station without a licence. Let us bear in mind what that means. It means that there will be no power left in the magistrate to decide that it has been a case of innocent oversight, a first offence, or a case simply for a nominal fine. In many cases the fines today are just fifty cents. It would thus become obligatory upon the magistrate, on summary conviction, to impose that minimum fine of $10. I ask the house if they are so wedded to that kind of licence fee that they are prepared to back up the Department of Transport in wanting to see conviction in a case of this kind punished by a minimum fine of $10. I think not.
The second proposal of the Department of Transport is that the Radio Act be further amended to eliminate some of the cumbersome procedure in connection with enforcement. That may be good if we are to continue with this present clumsy system. But I think there is a better way of meeting the needs of the situation; that is by doing away entirely with this nuisance tax.
The third proposal now being put forward by the Department of Transport as something designed to meet the needs of the situation was described before the committee by Mr. Browne on December 6. It involves the elimination of the house-to-house canvass, that source of revenue which produced 38.3 per cent of all the licence fees collected last year on account of receiving stations. In place of 346 people working full or part time in the field in the house-to-house canvass, the department proposes an increase in staff in the department, 42 people to be put in the field full time and 8 people to be added to the staff of the central records office at a cost to the department for the addition of 50 people to their staff, of about $100,000 per annum.
But that is not all. From the testimony of Mr. Browne it is evident that more hope is attached to their proposal to transfer the issuance of the receiving licences to the post offices to a greater extent than has ever been done hitherto. You are aware, sir, that at the present time the Department of Transport tries to issue or, if you like, to vend these licences through the post office. But Mr. Browne was frank enough to tell us in the committee that there has been much reluctance on the part of the post office and of individual post offices throughout the country to take on the task of collecting this $2.50 nuisance tax on behalf of the Department of Transport.
We are told that there are 1,600 staff post offices in Canada, 6,500 accounting post offices

Canadian Broadcasting Act and 5,000 non-accounting post offices. We are told that among the 1,600 staff post offices the carrying of these licences for those who may come in and seek to purchase them over the counter has become obligatory, but that on the part of the 6,500 accounting post offices the Department of Transport has found a great unwillingness to assume this task; and that in the case of the 5,000 non-accounting post offices there were, if you please, only 188 willing to take on this task at all. The other 4,800-odd simply refused to do so.
When the Department of Transport now proposes to look to the Post Office Department to take this unhappy task off their hands, it surely might have been well to ascertain in the first place whether the Posit Office Department was willing to do so. I am informed on good) authority, Mr. Chairman, that thie Post Office Department has not agreed to take on this task for the Department of Transport. Where does that leave uis? Let us forget for the moment the evidence of lack of co-operation between government departments or the attempt of one department to foist an unwelcome task on another government department. Does not this all point to the fact that this is a nuisance tax which ought to be eliminated? I have no doubt, sir, that if the committee heard the private opinions expressed by a good many government members there would not be much support left in this committee of the whole for the continued imposition of that $2.50 licence fee.
Let us look at some of the things that have been said by some of the more courageous members who had the temerity to express in the special committee an opinion on this subject. I refer now to the opinion expressed by the hon. member for Cariboo at the committee meeting of December 6. Mr. Browne made this comment:
. . . and they are the towns on which we concentrate first-
That is, on which the department concentrate their inspectors.
__when our prosecution campaign starts.
The hon. member for Cariboo said:
I am not urging you to prosecute them. I suggest it would be better to abolish the idea of a licence and to provide the money out of the general revenue because this is a public utility in which everybody shares and in which everybody enjoys the value; yet, according to your figures, half the people are not paying.

Then the hon. member for Saint John-Albert came before the committee. He was not a member, but he came before the committee and pointed out the curious situation which results from the way in which the fee is levied at the present time. The fee becomes payable on the 1st of April each year. The department does not issue any licences until April 1. It is not the system followed by the provincial governments in issuing motor vehicle licences. Here the licence cannot be issued until April 1. As the hon. member for Saint John-Albert pointed out, technically everybody is in default when the post office opens on April 1.
Then, if you please, none other than the Minister of National Revenue, at that same meeting to which I have referred, made some comments in which I think the committee would be interested. He said, in reviewing the proposal of the Department of Transport to foist this unhappy task of collecting the $2.50 licence fee on to the reluctant Post Office Department:
But I would be against the policy-if it is the policy-of not paying so much attention to the house-to-house canvassers and trying to increase the matter of prosecution.
The matter of prosecution is a very disagreeable thing to carry on. It only antagonizes people against those who are doing it, and I do not think that it is ever productive of any great results.
That is the verdict, sir, of the responsible minister who has had more to do with radio broadcasting in this country than any other minister. That is his comment upon proposals for shifting the collection of this $2.50 licence fee on to the Post Office Department, and his comments on the results of prosecutions for non-payment of the $2.50 licence fee.
This section does not propose simply to make a parliamentary grant this year; it proposes to set up a parliamentary grant for a five-year period year by year. I have said that the section is good in so far as it recognizes the principle of making direct parliamentary grants to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for its necessary purposes. It is sound to that extent, and to the extent to which the principle is sound, sir, I say to you it is then a condemnation in principle of the continued imposition of that $2.50 nuisance tax. If the principle of the parliamentary grant is sound, then it ought to be good enough for meeting all the needed revenues of the corporation. It is not, however, simply an annual grant, sir; it is a five-year grant that

we are asked to approve, and I for one say that the principle of a five-year grant in advance is not sound.
We have had abundant evidence in this debate, if indeed evidence were required, of the vital importance of preserving strict parliamentary control, as distinguished from governmental control, over the activities of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. When speaking on the resolution preceding the introduction of this bill several weeks ago 1 sought to urge that the principle of parliamentary control be vindicated in all circumstances with respect to radio broadcasting. There is not a danger that any one of us can conceive in this country, short of actual invasion by a totalitarian armed force, that would be a greater threat to democracy and freedom in Canada than for such a vitally important means of communication and dissemination of ideas and of shaping public thought as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to be brought under the control of the government. Therefore I say, sir, that parliament must be vigilant at all times to ensure that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation be divorced from government control, and that parliamentary control and parliamentary interest in the affairs of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation be strictly and sedulously maintained.
I say to you that if parliament makes a five-year grant in advance, committing itself to such a policy and to such grants by statute, it is making a mistake. It is risking a weakening in that parliamentary control over the corporation which is so essential, and the value of which is recognized by the officers of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
What seems to me should be the proper policy of parliament in this case is to make an annual grant to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to meet its needs. That will not prevent the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation from shaping its plans. I realize that plans cannot simply be circumscribed by any twelve-month period of time; but surely the board of governors of the corporation has enough confidence in parliament to know that parliament will make such provision as is required to meet the legitimate needs of the corporation. Sir, if the principle of five-year grants is sound, why not ten years? If the principle is sound with respect to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, why do we not apply it to the Canadian National Railways? We do not. We assert and preserve parliamentary control over the Canadian National Railways and their operations by insisting that parliament should, by annual grants, have an annual review to provide for the needs of that
Canadian Broadcasting Act corporation. Why should the same principle not be vindicated and preserved with respect to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation? Therefore I say to you that the proper method should be an annual grant to meet all the needs of the corporation, and that the item should appear in the estimates every year so that parliament will be acting consciously in making provision for the needs of the national system, and also so that the opportunity of discussing the affairs and reviewing the administration of the corporation every year will be guaranteed. It is not guaranteed here because we do not have a parliamentary committee set up every session. In view of the fact we have had one this session it may be unlikely that we will have one at the session of 1952; I do not know. But I do know, sir, that this year, as in so many years past, the report of the committee will come in too late for discussion. There will not be any opportunity given to the house for discussion of the report, and that is what will happen, it seems to me, in other future years even if you do have parliamentary committees, if this section is passed in its present form.
My final observation is this. Every one of us recognizes that broadcasting is going to cost money; that the kind of expansion which the officials of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation indicated in their very competent and willing review of their plans before the parliamentary committee is going to involve the expenditure of very large sums of money in these ensuing years. The grant contemplated by section 6 of this bill is not for television; it is simply for the expansion and development of sound broadcasting. The corporation will be looking to parliament to provide further funds for the development of television; and along with that we must bear in mind that up to the present -time at any rate the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has not been paying any taxes. It has not been paying any municipal taxes, even though the private stations with which it is competing directly for commercial revenues today have had to meet federal taxes, provincial taxes and municipal taxes.
Finally, sir, I say to you the issue that confronts the house now is one that I think is inescapable, because it is a challenge to the house. The issue is presented more clearly to the house with respect to the continuation of this $2.50 nuisance tax than on any occasion in any previous session; and if the house proceeds today to vindicate the principle of parliamentary grants then I say to you, sir, that it has destroyed any pretence of justification for a continuation of

Canadian Broadcasting Act that $2.50 licence fee. Far better that parliament should make the provision consciously, and do away with this nuisance tax.
To vindicate the policy of parliamentary control, sir, I move the following amendment:
That clause 6 of Bill 17 be amended by striking out all the words after the word "fifty-one" in line 7.
I point out to you, sir, that this will give to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation under this section $4,750,000 in this fiscal year. That will bring the direct parliamentary grants for this fiscal year to a total of $6,250,000, which is a sum substantially in excess of the amount the corporation can expend this year. It will provide for all their needs, for as much extension and expansion as they can possibly contemplate this year, and will leave them a substantial excess to carry over into the next fiscal year. But at the same time it will ensure the maintenance of parliamentary control with respect to the voting of parliamentary grants year by year in the future.

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF EXTENSIONS AND ADDITIONS TO THE BRITISH WEST INDIES TRADE LIBERALIZATION PLAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I may say that the timing of this announcement coincides with the timing of announcements being made in the United Kingdom and also in the British West Indies.
The United Kingdom has now authorized extensions and additions to the British West Indies trade liberalization plan, to take effect at the beginning of next year. Under this plan, limited quantities of traditional exports from dollar countries are being admitted to the markets of the British West Indies. It is estimated that some 650 firms have taken advantage of the present plan. The dollar value of the increased trade which will result from these new measures will not be large in total nor can it be estimated with any accuracy. For a number of Canadian exporters, however, it will provide a welcome opportunity to enter again into this trade. For others it will mean that increased quantities of their products will be admitted to those markets. All of this is definitely a step in the right direction. It is our great hope that further expansion will become possible in this trade in the future.
The British West Indies was the starting point for many of our manufacturers when they first looked abroad for export markets. There has been a tradition established of mutually advantageous trade. Because of the currency difficulties of the sterling area, British West Indian markets have unfortunately been closed to many of our goods since 1947. We have done our utmost in Canada, however, to provide a market for goods from the British West Indies, and from other countries in the sterling area, so that they might earn dollars with which to buy our goods. Canada has become a principal and substantial source of dollar earnings for these colonies. These efforts have obviously been recognized and appreciated in the United Kingdom, and I am happy to announce that we are now having increased opportunities being made available for Canadian goods in the British West Indies.
The government attaches great importance to our trade with the British West Indies. During 1950 we made strong representations to the United Kingdom for the creation of the

trade liberalization plan which was put into effect on January 1 of this year. Since then we have taken advantage of a number of opportunities to request the United Kingdom authorities to expand the existing arrangements. Members will recall that we had the honour in Ottawa in the early summer of being hosts to a visiting delegation of parliamentary representatives from various British West Indian colonies. The talks which took place at that time were useful to all parties concerned. When I visited London in September I made a special point of carrying the negotiations on this matter a further stage ahead, through direct contact with the appropriate ministers of the United Kingdom government.
The following statement is being made public today in the United Kingdom and Canada.
"Following discussions between the United Kingdom and Canadian governments and representatives of the British West Indies, which started early last summer, arrangements have now been worked out for extending and amending the existing scheme for 'token imports' into the British West Indies and Bahamas from Canada and the United States.
So far as the Canadian side is concerned, from 1st January, 1952, the list of items covered by the scheme has been expanded to include a much wider range of commodities, including food products, leather, metal, electrical and textile manufactures, etc. Also the percentages for exporters' quotas for most of these commodities will be raised from 33 J per cent to 40 per cent.
The expanded trade liberalization arrangements will, as from the 1st January, 1952, operate differently for British West Indies and Bahamas trade with the United States. Instead of a system of commodity quotas based on a percentage of past trade,, the West Indies and Bahamas will be able to licence additional imports from the United States up to a specified total value.
North American exports should also benefit from the authority recently given for colonial governments to introduce a system of world open general licences for certain commodities. These are mainly of a kind essential to colonial development. The list of goods to which open general licences may be applied covers for example a wide range of finished steel items 'and1 semi-manufactures of copper, zinc, and nickel but also includes dried, pickled, salted and smoked fish, onions, potatoes, certain animal feeding stuffs and jute goods.
Trade with British West Indies
In spite of the grave balance of payments position of the sterling area, it has been thought right to recognize in these arrangements the great importance of good commercial relations between the British West Indies and North America and they represent a substantial easing of import restrictions on goods exported by Canada and the United States."
I would like to conclude by tabling a more detailed statement, which has been prepared for the use of the press.

precedent and which-and I am trying to use moderate language-outrages one of the basic principles of our method of financing. I want to read from page 44 of a book by Durell on "Parliamentary Grants". I am going to read about half a page. I do not like reading, but I think this is a matter of importance. I understand it was once said of Lloyd George: Presumably he can read and write, though he gives no sign of ever having done either. The late Mr. J. W. Dafoe told me that one day at Paris he saw Mr. Lloyd George go into the assembly and pick up Le Temps. Somebody saw him reading it and said, "He can read, he can read French." It is lucky for hon. members that I am not reading French. I will read English. The passage is as follows:
The grants made by the House of Commons may be classified under two main heads: those which are authorized as recurring direct charges on the consolidated fund, and those which are met by annual or special vote for the supply services. Direct charges on the consolidated fund, which amount to about a third of the annual expenditure, are authorized by statute . . . When once granted they become in effect continuing grants to the treasury . . . They do not come up for annual review or criticism, and are to that extent removed from the control of the House of Commons after the statute has been passed. On the other hand it is at any time within the power of parliament to repeal such a statute and to transform the charge from a permanent one to an annual one . . . The fact, however, of the charges not being automatically brought under review necessarily withdraws them in a measure from the notice of parliament, and there is a disinclination consequently to make such permanent charges in any cases which could be provided for without detriment by an annual vote.
Then there is one short paragraph under the heading "Annual Estimates". It reads:
The remainder of the expenditure set forth in the budget is in the form of proposals which require to be voted for the service of the year, and it is in the exercise of its function of granting these supplies that the supreme control of the House of Commons is most evident.
I have gone through the estimates not meticulously but with what care I could in the time available, and so far as I can discover there is no case that in the least resembles this. We have statutory grants of course for the service of the debt, the payment of the salaries of cabinet ministers, subsidies, grants to the provinces and various thinks of that kind, but I cannot find anything which in the least resembles the kind of grant that we have before us. I am not able to

imagine any reason whatever why it cannot be dealt with in the ordinary way unless for the reason that those who are responsible do not want to face the proper test of coming forward each year. I do not imagine the minister will give that as a reason, but I hope he can give a much better reason than certainly I imagine he possibly can.
I have not had time to search through Hansard as I would have liked to, but I can well imagine the kind of things that would have been said in this house, and in particular by the leader of the opposition in the years between 1930 and 1935, if there had been any attempt to depart from a well recognized, well established, well understood and perfectly reasonable method of financing. I hope if the committee passes this section they will not do so in ignorance. If I am correct- and if I am not the minister will no doubt do his best to correct me-they will by so doing create an evil precedent which will no doubt be invoked again and again on other occasions. I still hope it may be possible that the minister will change his mind.
