I shall only take a few minutes of the time of the committee, but I wish to say a word or two on this particular section of the bill. Before I deal with what I was intending to discuss I should like to add a word or two to what the hon. member for Eglinton said this afternoon with respect to the discontinuance of the radio licence fee. I do not know that I am especially fussy one way or the other, but I want to point out particularly that a number of people have advocated to the public the doing away with the licence fee. What the hon. member for Eglinton really is saying in principle is not that we will do away with the licence fee but that because it is a nuisance tax we will shift it into the general taxation policy of the country and not call it a licence fee. I mention this because I think we need to point out that during election campaigns many aspirants to membership in this house have appeared on election platforms giving the people the impression that if they are elected they will advocate doing away with the licence fee. To my mind that may be technically correct, but since that same amount of money will have to be made up in some way those people should be fair and add that everyone will be taxed accordingly. That much more money will have to be raised, and therefore all citizens will share in it whether or not they own a radio. One thing we must remember is that under the present system of licensing it is the person who owns the radio receiving set who pays the licence fee, and the person who does not own a radio set does not pay the licence fee. Under the system
Canadian Broadcasting Act advocated now, whether or not a person owned a radio set he would have to pay his share of the over-all taxation to make up that $5 million annually.
The point I really intended to make on this section which we are now asked to pass is that the people of Canada will have to pay to the C.B.C. about $30 million over a period of five years. Now, $30 million is a lot of money. In addition to that $30 million the C.B.C. also receives around $5 million per year from the radio licence fees. This will mean that by the end of that five-year period the C.B.C. will have received from the taxpayers of Canada about $55 million. I mention that for the purpose of making this further observation. During the radio committee's hearings a brief was presented by the Canadian association of broadcasters, which represents the bulk of the independent stations in Canada. During the sessions of the committee the spokesman for the association, Mr. Allard, whom no one will say was not an able witness, was asked this question: If the independent stations could so organize themselves and mobilize their forces as to give Canada a national system of radio, while at the same time giving the Canadian public the high standard of radio it now enjoys, could they do that without any cost to the taxpayer? Mr. Allard's answer was yes.
Before commenting any further, I take it that answer was given by a man who knew what he was talking about. I do not believe anyone on the committee would say that Mr. Allard did not speak with some considerable authority about radio. Yet his opinion was that private radio, by mobilizing these stations and its organizations, could give Canada a national system of radio such as it has today, at least without depreciating the calibre or quality of the programs and yet without any expense to the taxpayers. It is only fair that I should mention that the president of the board of governors appeared as a subsequent witness. I called Mr. Allard's answer to that question to his attention, and I asked Mr. Dunton if he had any comment to make. He said that his comment would be as terse as Mr. Allard's comment, but instead of saying yes he would say no. No one will doubt that Mr. Dunton also is qualified to speak on behalf of radio, at least on behalf of the C.B.C. He is in a position to know. What we have here is a conflict of opinion as between two men whom one would regard as radio experts.
My point is this. Even though there is some conflict of opinion, and even though Mr. Allard's statement might be regarded by some as exaggerated, nevertheless it was made. Even though we grant that statement might be exaggerated, the C.B.C. would still

Canadian Broadcasting Act have an advantage over Mr. Allard's proposal to the tune of at least the radio licence fees of $5 million a year. They would have that amount of money over and above what Mr. Allard said the independent stations in Canada could actually give Canada. I point that out because I think it is an observation we need to keep in mind.
Now, $5 million is a lot of money to spend on radio in one year, expecially when radio is a competitive business and the C.B.C. is in the commercial field. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation say they have to have more than that. They have to have an additional $6 million. The people of Canada should know that they are paying $5 million a year in radio licence fees as a straight gift to the C.B.C. It is an amount that they have-I was going to say to play with, but that might be too loose an expression-but they have that much leeway over and above what the independent stations would need. Then there is another point, and it may be a meagre point. The independent stations would still have to pay their taxes, while the C.B.C. today is largely free of taxation andt has that advantage over the independent stations.
The bill, of course, says the taxpayer must not only pay the $5 million in licence fees; he must pay another $6 million a year. I point out that observation. Personally I should like to see the C.B.C. develop just as far as it is possible for them to develop. But if the C.B.C. were a private corporation charged with the responsibility of giving Canada the standard of radio that is given today, I am quite certain that as a private corporation they could get along with far less than an additional amount of about $11 million a year which they are asking from the taxpayers. I say that in the light of the fact that we have one man's opinion to the effect that if radio were in private hands, they could do it without any cost to the taxpayers whatsoever.

The matter under discussion at the present time has to do with the amendment of the hon. member for Eglinton with reference to the new revenue arrangements for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and these are in line with the recommendations of the commission. Let me point out that they provide for the payment to the corporation of a fixed sum of $6,250,000 each year for a period of five years. It is estimated that these payments, together with the receipts from the receiving licence fees and commercial operations, will bring the annual revenue of the corporation to about the equivalent of one dollar per head of the population of Canada. This is the amount which, in the opinion of the commission, will be needed by the national broadcasting system to maintain its services and carry out some necessary improvements in the five-year period.
I should like to point out that the commission recommended the annual fee for radio licensed sets be maintained at its present level, but that a more effective method of collection be devised.
The hon. member has issued a challenge to give reasons why this policy should be followed. I accept this challenge immediately,

Canadian Broadcasting Act and I think probably I can free his mind of any objection he might have. It has been suggested by him and by other hon. members that payments should not be set now by statute for a five-year period, but should be voted annually by parliament. That is the gist of the amendment. The chief argument for such an annual vote seemed to be that it would provide parliament each year with an opportunity to review the affairs of the C.B.C. I should like to say that I for one am in favour of frequent reviews by parliament of the matters and affairs of the corporation. Not to nay knowledge has a request for the annual setting up of a committee on radio broadcasting been denied. It is true that it has not been held every year, but as far as my memory goes it has never been denied when it has been requested.
I think it is a good thing that every year, or every year it seems fit, this house should appoint a committee for this purpose. With the appointment of such a committee there is ample opportunity for discussion by the whole house of the activities of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, its aims and objectives.
I believe there are two strong arguments against the annual vote of money for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The first I think was well put by the royal commission itself when it said:
There are, however, serious objections to an annual grant to be voted by parliament. Although other essential government services depend on an annual vote, it is so important to keep the national radio free from the possibility of political influence that its income should not depend annually on direct action by the government of the day.
I have heard expressed in this house countless times, when radio matters were up, the fear, the accusation and the challenge that the government was interfering politically with the operations of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I think another important principle is involved here, with which I thought hon. members on the opposition side of the house would agree. They have stated that they are in agreement with us on insistence that the activities of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should not come under the direct influence of the government of the day. Under the provisions of the bill before the committee there would be no question of the government having influence on the operations of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation through the power of proposing votes of money for operating purposes each year. As I say, however, I believe that although payments to the corporation from public funds will not be voted annually, parliament will still have plenty


of opportunity to examine the affairs of the corporation to which it is directly responsible, and I think should do so.
The second reason for a fixed sum for a period of five years is that it will enable the corporation to make proper plans on a reasonably long-term basis. When the corporation was set up by parliament it was the idea that it should manage its affairs on a businesslike basis, following as closely as possible the methods of private operations, as is necessary in the field of broadcasting.
The hon. gentleman made reference to the fact that this was not done in the days of the Bennett government from 1930 to 1935. No, certainly it was not. Let me draw the attention of the committee to the fact that in the annual statement of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation it was not until 1946 that it was necessary to secure a loan that still remains unpaid. There were loans on many occasions during the period from 1932 to 1946, but every one of those loans was repaid by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. They were repaid not by taxes on the general public but by the people who were served and through their annual receiving set fee and the fees of private stations. They were able to save enough money out of that to redeem those loans.

I do not think that broadcasting is the kind of activity for which estimates can be worked out each year in

the same way they can for government departments. In broadcasting, particularly in Canada, there are-and very probably there always will be-many demands from different sections of the public for more of something, particularly in the program field where there are many different opinions about what expenditures are necessary.
It seems to me that the sensible thing for parliament to do is to tell the corporation what its sources of revenue will be for the next five years, and set a reasonable amount in relation to the economy of the country. Then it is the responsibility of the corporation, which will report here yearly, to spend that money to the greatest possible advantage, subject always to a review by parliament.
The hon. member for Yale spoke with reference to the services in the particular district in which he resides. I admit immediately that his district is entitled to better services, and I promise that it will get better services if the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has the money with which to give them. This is all a matter of finance. The physical part of it can be attended to. There are no technical difficulties in the way of giving better services, but because of the fact that the C.B.C. has not had sufficient revenue it has not been able to give the services to several communities to which these people are entitled.

I wish to refer to subsections 6 and 7, which are set out in subsection 2 of section 7. I shall not repeat the argument made this afternoon, that one of the matters respecting which there has been much criticism generally throughout the country has been the fact that in the

relationship prevailing as between the corporation and the private stations no provision is made for the adjudication of disputes as between the corporation and the private stations. Indeed the corporation is in the position of making regulations, making the law as it were, interpreting the law and deciding on conflicts or disagreements as between the corporation and the private stations.
Many of us have advocated the setting up of a board similar to the board of transport commissioners in order to assure that as between the corporation and the private stations there will be a measure of equity, and the administration of justice will be preserved. However, that has not been accepted. Apparently with a desire to go part of the way provision is made in subsection 7 of section 7 that where the corporation orders the suspension of the licence of a private station under subsection 6, the licensee may by leave of a judge of the Exchequer Court of Canada appeal against such order to the said court on any question of law.
That right of appeal to the exchequer court is limited and circumscribed to such an extent as to be meaningless and ineffectual to all intents and purposes. It covers only the right of a private station to aDpeal when its licence is suspended or cancelled, only to leave, and onlv in the event that a question of law is involved.
I am not saying at the moment that there are cases where prejudice or bias would enter into the determination by the corporation, ais to whether a private station should not have its licence suspended. As it now stands this section will have the effect of continuing in the corporation its psychological power of interfering with any particular private station one might name; and that private station will be in the position, if it does anything that is contrary to the regulations of the corporation, of being subject to the cancellation or abrogation or suspension of its licence. It would have no appeal. If there is bias or prejudice in the cancellation of the licence there would be no right of appeal. There is only a right of appeal, regardless of what the equities or facts may be, provided there has been a mistake in law or provided a point of law is at issue as between the corporation and the private station.
In order to provide an appeal on fact as well as on law in connection with all orders made by the C.B.C., I move, seconded by the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Cardiff):
That subsection 7 of section 7 be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"Any person affected by any order, direction or ruling of the corporation may appeal to the Exchequer Court of Canada against such order, direction

or ruling on any question of law or fact or mixed question of law and fact, and the said court may stay the operation of such order, direction or ruling pending its final decision and said court may affirm, alter or rescind the order, direction or ruling appealed from."
Under that amendment the effect would be that if the C.B.C. made an order or a ruling as against a private station under which that station felt aggrieved, it would have the right to appeal to the exchequer court. While that court is of lower jurisdiction than the Supreme Court of Canada in general, it is composed of men who have the necessary judicial capacity to determine whether or not an order that has been made is fair and reasonable or whether it is one that is inequitable, unjust and unjustifiable.
This amendment would provide for an appeal by the private station, but it would in no way weaken the C.B.C. After all the stand of the corporation is that it in no way does anything that is unjust to the private stations. If it does not, it has nothing to worry about as to the right of appeal. If it does, being in the position of a competitor, as was brought out this afternoon, by reason of both the corporation and the private broadcasting company being engaged in an endeavour to secure advertising, then in order to assure justice the private station surely should have the right of recourse to the courts.
It is all very well to say that the corporation will not do wrong and does not do wrong. There is no court, except the final court, in any land that ascribes to itself infallibility in its judgments or decisions. Courts make mistakes; that is why there are appeal courts. Surely we are not going to ascribe to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation a higher degree of infallibility than the courts possess, particularly when in many cases its judgment is based on a complaint or on a subject of controversy with its competitor, the private station.
While this amendment does not suggest the setting up of an independent body such as we on this side of the house have advocated over the years, one in the nature of the board of transport commissioners which adjudicates as between the government owned railroad and the privately owned railroad, it would provide, first, an alternative to such a board and, second, the assurance that both the C.B.C. and the private broadcasting company as co-litigants in a proceeding before the court would be assured of justice and at the same time any suggestion of bias, prejudice, intimidation or the psychological effect of the private company being subject to the control of the C.B.C., both as a competitor and in an adjudicating position, would be removed.
Canadian Broadcasting Act
On the face of it this amendment would remove any and every possible cause of complaint. It would assure justice. It would preserve the rule of law. It would maintain a relationship between the corporation and the private broadcasting companies that would inure to the benefit of broadcasting in Canada.

Before it carries, I was not a member of the radio committee and probably the question I am going to ask was brought up before, but I should like to ask the minister why the word "alleged" is introduced in line 21. The clause now reads:
In case of any alleged violation or non-observance by a private station of the regulations made by the corporation under this section, the corporation may, after notice has been given to the licensee of the alleged violation or non-observance and an opportunity afforded to the licensee to be heard . . .
The corporation may then suspend the licence. I should think the suspension of the licence of a private radio station is the most stringent action that could be taken against it. As a matter of fact it puts the private station out of business. It would seem to me that before a private station is put out of business there certainly should be a proved case of violation or non-observance, and that an alleged violation should not be good enough. As the clause now reads it would seem to me all that is necessary is for somebody to allege that a violation has taken place; and if the private station does not produce proof, which may be very difficult for it to do, that it has not been guilty of a violation then its licence is suspended. I should like to know why it was felt necessary to introduce the word "alleged". It seems to me it is entirely unnecessary, and puts the private station in an almost hopeless position. In other words it goes directly contrary to all our usually accepted ideas of the law, namely that a person accused must be proven guilty. In this case the person accused has to prove that he is not guilty, otherwise he loses his licence.

As far as I can see it is for the specific purpose of putting the person against whom the violation is alleged at a disadvantage. It puts him in the position where he has to prove his innocence rather than leaving it, as has always been the case under our law, that the people alleging the crime or violation must prove that he is guilty.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADVANCE POLLS AND PRISONERS OF WAR VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Having been a member of the elections act committee, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few observations at this stage. Before so doing I must gently chide the genial Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) for some remarks he made last night when he was informing us of the business of the house. The minister said:
Tomorrow we will continue the consideration of Bill No. 17, to amend the Canadian Broadcasting Act, 1936, and then a list of small bills: Bill No. 41, to amend the Dominion Elections Act . . .
I am quite sure this house does not consider this a small bill. It is not small in physical size, because it contains 50 pages. It is not small in content because it contains a great deal of material which is the result of much study on the part of the committee. It is not small in importance because it is the statutory provision governing the election of members to this house. I am sure it is not a small bill in any sense of the word so far' as hon. members of this house are concerned.
I want to say that I have enjoyed working on the elections committee, both during the last session and this session. I particularly appreciate the non-partisan approach of the members of the committee in giving consideration to this very important legislation. The committee went through the act thoroughly from beginning to end. First of all we received the advice and suggestions of the chief electoral officer, Mr. Castonguay, as his experience had indicated there should be technical and other changes. Then the hon. members of this house presented to the committee the results of their personal experience, and their knowledge of conditions in various parts of Canada. I am sure the combination of the experience of the chief electoral officer and the experience of the members resulted in satisfactory amendments to this act.
Before proceeding with the sections of the act with which I wish to deal this evening, I do wish to pay a tribute to our chief electoral officer, Mr. Castonguay. I was very much impressed with his knowledge of the act and the completely detached and objective way in which he carries out his duties. Without doubt the majority of Canadians believe the chief electoral officer is some part of parliament's administrative machinery. He is not necessarily a personality they know. I am sure if they realized the objective way and the spirit in which our chief electoral officer carries out his duties they would have a very high appreciation of the great function he performs in a parliamentary democracy.

Doviinion Elections Act
We in this group consider this bill generally satisfactory. We believe it is a most important measure because it is the foundation upon which the machinery of democracy functions. The other day I read newspaper comments concerning the limited knowledge and information of university students about the working of our democracy. They were asked who the Prime Minister of Canada was, and so on, and it was obvious from these newspaper reports that a lot of university students do not know who the Prime Minister of Canada is. These students lack other information relating to this house. I believe this indicates some lack in our educational system. In my, opinion every high school student in Canada should be taught the terms of the British North America Act. In learning those terms the student would have a complete knowledge of constitutional developments in Canada, and of Canadian history. I believe everyone should have a thorough understanding of the Canadian Citizenship Act and of the elections act. Those three acts are fundamental and must be understood by a large percentage of our people if they are going to have a proper appreciation of the democracy we enjoy.
I am going to devote the rest of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, to a subject about which I am quite concerned, and about which a proportion of the constituents I represent are concerned. According to the elections act now, and the provincial legislation of British Columbia, certain persons of Doukhobor origin are denied the franchise.
I am going to bring briefly to the attention of the committee a misunderstanding I found in the elections act committee when I first approached the matter. There seems to be a misunderstanding generally throughout the country, occasioned largely by improper reporting of the circumstances that exist in Kootenay West. I am going to deal briefly with that question as related to the elections act.
There is no question about it, no other immigrant group in Canada presented such a spectacular problem to federal and provincial governments as the Doukhobors, who are a religious sect of Russian origin. There are some seven or eight thousand Doukhobors in Saskatchewan and Alberta who have become more or less successfully adapted to their Canadian environment. There are some ten to twelve thousand persons of Doukhobor origin in Kootenay West and adjacent districts. In order to inform hon. members correctly I must explain that the Doukhobors in British Columbia consist of three main groups. First there is the orthodox element of some six thousand persons, the majority of whom belong to the Union of


Spiritual Communities of Christ and live in the area surrounding the village of Brilliant. These people represent the heart of the Doukhobor community and are a group who aim to retain their traditional language, culture and religious beliefs while making a peaceful adjustment to the Canadian way of life.
Then we have the independent element numbering about three to four thousand persons. This element is composed of individual Doukhobors who have become partially or entirely assimilated. While many of them still pay lip service to the traditional Doukhobor beliefs, they have severed their former ties with Doukhobor organizations and occupy their own properties in the cities and in the country. This is the group that I want to deal with briefly in relation to this bill, Mr. Speaker. Then, finally, there is the group known as the Sons of Freedom, numbering something over two thousand persons. They are uncompromising Doukhobor fundamentalists who tend to react violently against any forces in the Canadian environment which they feel threatens their traditional Doukhobor values. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, with many Canadians the Doukhobor problem tends to be identified almost entirely with the activities of the Sons of Freedom, who refuse to pay rent or taxes and are technically squatters on provincial land.
In 1950, as a result of the disturbances occasioned by the Sons of Freedom, a consultative committee for British Columbia was established under the chairmanship of Dr. MacKenzie, president of the university of British Columbia, composed of several of the staff of that university and representatives nominated by boards of trade at Nelson, Trail and Grand Forks. Before proceeding further, may I say that this committee was formed to study the whole Doukhobor question and make recommendations to the government of British Columbia.
From a personal knowledge of the local situation and a personal knowledge of what these people are doing, I must express my appreciation of the work of the members of the committee, and of the outstanding work that is being performed by former Commissioner Mead of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, former Commissioner Shirras, of the provincial police, and to the Society of Friends, for allowing Mr. Gulley, one of the former United Nations relief administrators in Arabia, to come to the Kootenays to assist in solving this question. I must also express my appreciation of the work being done by the ministerial association of the Nelson district. Only recently I read of a meeting

where large numbers of these people were gathered together with other segments of the population in an effort to bring those two groups together. I must say, Mr. Chairman, that the meetings have been successful to date. There is no question about it that part of the difficulties in Kootenay West are created by the lack of interest other Canadians have taken in the problem they created in the years gone by.
I am also informed that officials of the minister's department are co-operating in this work and have attended meetings to discuss this question with interested persons. I hope this work will continue and be extended, because it presents a great challenge and opportunity to the citizenship branch of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration.
Now that I have briefly reviewed the question may I say that I rise this evening to speak particularly on one aspect of the Douk-hobor problem, namely the great injustice that is continued by the denial of the franchise to this group of independents and others of Doukhobor origin. The statutes of British Columbia prevent a Doukhobor or a person of Doukhobor descent from voting in a provincial election. I want to quote from those statutes. I quote revised statutes of 1948, chapter 106, provincial elections act."
Definition of Doukhobor:	Doukhobor means a
person, male or female, exempted or entitled to claim exemption or who on production of any certificate might have become or would now be entitled to claim exemption from military service by reason of the order of the governor in council of December sixth, 1898, and every descendent of any such person, whether born in the province or elsewhere . . .
Then section 4, clause E, of the provincial elections act, disqualifies "every Doukhobor or person of Doukhobor descent, providing that the provisions of this clause shall not disqualify or render incompetent to vote any person of Doukhobor origin who served in His Majesty's forces" and so on. They are not allowed to vote in a provincial election. Section 14 of the Dominion Elections Act and of the act before us now, the Canada Elections Act, reads as follows:
(2) The following persons are disqualified from voting at an election and incapable of being registered as electors and shall not vote nor be so registered, that is to say-
. . . (j) In any province, every person exempted or entitled to claim exemption or who on production of any certificate might have become or would now be entitled to claim exemption from military service by reason of the order in council of December sixth, 1898, because the doctrines of his religion make him averse to bearing arms, and who is by the law of {hat province disqualified from voting at an election of a member of the legis-tive assembly of that province.
As a result of this combination of provincial and federal legislation, so far as elections
Dominion Elections Act are concerned some considerable group of persons of Doukhobor ancestry are prevented from exercising the franchise, regardless of the fact that they are willing to accept the full responsibilities of a Canadian citizen. What are the types of persons disqualified? There are a good many persons of Doukhobor ancestry who are completely detached from the Doukhobor community and are working in industries in my constituency, but who are not permitted to exercise the franchise in Canada. There are businessmen in my constituency, members of boards of trade, members of Rotary and other service clubs, members of churches-members, I think, of several churches to which members of the House of Commons belong-who are absolutely denied the franchise because they are of Doukhobor origin. I have, of course, in my constituency a number of university graduates, doctors of philosophy, masters of arts, bachelors of science, who are denied the franchise because they are of Doukhobor descent, but who have completely divorced themselves from the Doukhobor community.
In addition I know of a number of Doukhobor parents who persuaded their sons to join the armed forces during the second world war. There were considerable numbers of Doukhobors in the armed forces. Anyone who understands the Doukhobors realizes that that is something for the parents of young Doukhobors to do. Regardless of their desire-and in that case, from their point of view, an extreme demonstration of their desire-to be Canadian citizens, those parents at the present time are denied the franchise.
Then again, the grandchildren of Doukhobors whose grandmothers were Canadians of united empire loyalist stock are denied the franchise under the present legislation. I am speaking particularly of this group of three or four thousand persons, the independents, who are not associated with the orthodox community and are completely opposed to and dissociated from the Sons of Freedom. Mr. Speaker, in Saskatchewan and, I think, in every other province in Canada these people are permitted the franchise; that is, people of Doukhobor origin who are willing to accept the responsibilities of Canadian citizenship. I am making this particular appeal to the house tonight with the realization that it is not possible to secure an amendment to the act at the present time. I do so in order to inform hon. members of the situation so that when this act comes under revision in the near future, and when circumstances are opportune, something will be done about this continuing injustice.

Recently in the Ontario legislature a bill was introduced with respect to certain trade union legislation, and the United Nations declaration of human rights was quoted by the minister presenting that legislation to the house as one of the reasons the legislation was being introduced. I presented this situation to the elections act committee, and after I made a very similar explanation to that which I have made here this evening I was very pleased to see that committee members were sympathetic to my representations, and understood the question much more fully than they had prior to that time. When the committee presented its report on June 27, 1951 they included in it the resolution I had moved and which the committee had adopted as follows:
That the government give consideration to extending the franchise to certain persons of Douk-hobor origin and the advisability of consultation with the government of the province of British Columbia in this matter.
The committee met this session. This bill is the result of their meeting. I took the opportunity then to raise the question and find out what had happened. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris) very kindly stated this to the committee:
The committee at the last session passed a resolution which asked the government to give consideration to apDroaching the provincial government of British Columbia with respect to the possible voting of Doukhobors. The form of the resolution was such that we did not feel any compulsion to approach them; it was merely that we would give consideration to approaching them, and we did that. Having in mind, however, that at this particular time the question of the movement of the Doukhobors from one location to another was a matter of some concern to the people in British Columbia as well as to the government we felt that

we would be injecting another note which possibly might not be to the advantage of the government in solving what I think we all agree is a very difficult problem, and, accordingly, we have not ap-proacned them. I hope that statement has nothing in it in any way discourteous to the mover of the resolution, because it has only been carried to that extent, but it is felt that this is not the time that such a matter should be proceeded with.

Mr. Jean-Fran^ois Poulioi (Temiscouata):
Mr. Speaker, looking at today's order paper, we notice that the French version of this bill has not been produced. Since it is a translation and because there is even one section of the bill, section 58, where new French expressions are used, it seems important to me that we should have both versions of the bill, especially the French version, so that we may know exactly what designation is given to the same functions.
The other day I spoke somewhat heatedly of the translation of laws. I will read section 58-I have just now received, the French version of the bill-where it is seen that certain changes were madie in the new legislation:
The French version of the said act is amended by striking out the expressions "officier-rappor-teur" "sous-officier rapporteur", "officier rapporteur special" and "sous-officier rapporteur special" wherever they appear herein and substituting therefor, in each case, the expressions "directeur du scrutin", "sous-directeur du scrutin" and "sous-directeur special du scrutin", respectively.

The latter terms are unknown to those who look after the administration and enforcement of the elections act throughout the country. At all times, town clerks and others have been appointed "sous-officiers rapporteurs" (deputy returning officers)-that is how they have always been called-and it seems to me that when a French or English expression is sanctioned in the act, it should become a Canadian expression.
I understand that in the United States, whenever even a slang expression has been in the statutes for twenty-five years, it becomes official. I feel that here this is not necessary, and one cannot say that certain French terms are anglicisms, as long as they are accepted and authorized by the act.
I wonder why changes are made in terms and phrases that have iheir place and, especially, have a meaning. But what strikes me most, Mr. Speaker-and I will quote only one instance here-is that two different terms are used in the act to designate the same thing. For instance, on page 124 of Votes and Proceedings, in rule 33, the revising officer is called a "reviseur", while on page 120 he is called an "officier reviseur". That is very odd.
It seems to me the designation applied to someone carrying out the same duties should always be the same and, in my opinion, the use of two different designations is apt to be confusing.
I have also noticed that, in many sections, the French version of the act is bilingual since certain terms belong to the French language while others belong to the language of bureaucracy. Whenever a designation belonging to the language of bureaucracy is used, ''expression frangaise" is put in parentheses as an explanation or comment, in order that people may not be too baffled.
I will not insist too much on this subject since I do not intend to take up too much of the time of the house. But, Mr. Speaker, the question is extremely serious since I have the greatest respect for the law and I hold that it should be as immutable as possible.
In many circumstances I have complained of the far too great number of amendments made to the law. It runs past our eyes like a film. It lacks stability and that greatly affects jurisprudence.
Still, Mr. Speaker, I do take some consolation from the reading of the amendments to the elections act. Electors are not called 94699-122J
Dominion Elections Act "commettants" but "electeurs". It seems to me that immense progress has been made. In Hansard electors are called "commettants", here they are called "electeurs"; that is some progress anyway. I will not stop there; I warn the house against the work of translators in general. I am informed that in the translation of the Criminal Code, from English into French, there are a great many new expressions which will contribute a great deal to confuse all those who have to interpret and enforce the law. I hope the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson), who is now in his seat, will see to it that no changes are made in the terms now used in the French version of the Criminal Code and of the other statutes. Statutory law is complicated enough as it is now and, in my opinion, it would be absurd to make it absolutely incomprehensible by using new expressions unknown to and not understood by the public.
Tonight I have appealed, as best I could, to the common sense of my colleagues and to the legal experience of those whom it is my privilege to number among my fellow members of the bar. It is my hope that each one of them will see to it that those who want to do better than others are prevented from defacing or mutilating the law.
